text: Preface

title: NebulaStream: A Stream Processing Engine from the Inside Out
text:
What this book is
There are good textbooks on databases. There is no textbook on a single modern stream processing engine.
Garcia-Molina, Ullman and Widom’s Database Systems: The Complete Book will teach you relational algebra, SQL, B-trees and the canonical query optimizer. Petrov’s Database Internals will guide you through storage engines and distributed consensus. Kleppmann’s Designing Data-Intensive Applications will give you the conceptual map of the data-systems landscape, batch and stream alike. None of them takes a single streaming system, opens it up, and walks you through what is actually inside.
This book does that, using NebulaStream as the specimen. NebulaStream is an end-to-end data-management system for cloud-edge-sensor deployments, developed jointly at BIFOLD by the DIMA Group at TU Berlin and the DFKI IAM Group. It is written in C++23, generates native code for every query through a custom JIT framework called Nautilus, and is designed from the ground up to run across the full sensor-fog-cloud spectrum.
We will not pretend NebulaStream is the only or best stream processing engine. We chose it because it is small enough to be tractable, large enough to be interesting, and unusually well-documented in tree. The techniques you will see — code generation, watermarks, two-queue schedulers, plugin registries — appear in Flink, in Materialize, in Arroyo, in Hyper. NebulaStream is the worked example. The lessons generalize.

title: NebulaStream: A Stream Processing Engine from the Inside Out
text:
What this book is not
It is not a user manual. If you want to learn how to write a SELECT statement against NebulaStream, the official documentation will serve you better.
It is not a comparative survey. Tyler Akidau, Slava Chernyak and Reuven Lax wrote Streaming Systems for that. We will compare to other engines in short, well-bounded sidebars when the comparison illuminates a NebulaStream design choice, and not otherwise.
It is not a course in distributed systems theory. We assume you know why a leader election matters, what linearizability is, and why networks partition. Where NebulaStream’s design depends on a particular theoretical result, we cite the paper and move on.

title: NebulaStream: A Stream Processing Engine from the Inside Out
text:
How to read it
The book is organised into five parts.
Part I: Foundations establishes the vocabulary. You will see how a SQL query becomes native code in roughly forty pages. The remaining twenty-one chapters fill in the steps.
Part II: The Query Frontier covers the path from text to a logical plan: parser, algebra, time and watermarks, sources and sinks.
Part III: Optimization and Compilation covers the path from a logical plan to executable native code: rule-based optimizer, physical lowering, pipelining, JIT code generation.
Part IV: Runtime and Execution covers what happens when the generated code starts processing tuples: task scheduling, state management, error handling, the worker process.
Part V: Operations and Frontiers covers everything around the engine: distributed deployment, testing, benchmarking, open research problems.
Most chapters depend on Part I but are otherwise reasonably independent. If you are interested in code generation, jump to Chapter 12. If you are interested in scheduling, jump to Chapter 15. The full chapter graph is in 1.6 Reading order.

A note on currency
NebulaStream is an actively developed engine. The codebase moves; design documents do not. An earlier revision of this manuscript anchored several chapters on the in-tree docs/design/ documents — which are dated 2024 — as if they described 2026 reality. They do not. The implementation has evolved significantly past several of those design documents, most visibly in the distribution layer (Chapter 19), where what was research roadmap in 2024 is the production data plane in 2026.
Chapter 19 has been rewritten to reflect this; smaller adjustments appear in Chapters 1, 2, 13, 14, 16, 18, and 22. The rule we have settled on for the rest of the manuscript: design documents are historical context; the live code is authoritative. Where we cite a design document, we cite it for the rationale it captures, not as a description of current state. The book’s scripts/drift-check.py verifies that file paths and line ranges still resolve, but it cannot verify that narratives still match behaviour. That part requires maintainer review.

title: 1  Why Stream Processing? Why Another Engine?
text:
1.1 1.1 A short history of streaming engines
The history of database systems is, in a coarse approximation, a history of attempts to deal with data that does not fit. Data that does not fit in main memory motivated the buffer manager. Data that does not fit on one disk motivated partitioning. Data that does not fit in one transaction motivated isolation levels. And data that does not fit inside a query — that arrives, continuously, while the query runs — motivated stream processing.
This is a book about a particular stream processing engine. Before we open it up, though, we should be honest about why such engines exist, why we keep building new ones, and why NebulaStream is worth a book of its own.
The first generation of streaming systems were academic. Aurora (2003), Borealis (2005) and TelegraphCQ (2003) established that a continuous query — a query that runs forever, producing a continuous answer — was a coherent mathematical object, not just a hack on top of a relational DBMS. They taught us about windowing, watermarks, and what it meant for a query to “complete” without ever stopping.
The second generation went into production. Apache Storm (2011), later Apache Flink (2015), Apache Spark Streaming (2013) and Kafka Streams (2016) brought streaming to industry. They solved the operational problems the academic systems left open — checkpointing, exactly-once processing, scaling to thousands of nodes, integration with the Hadoop and Kafka ecosystems. But they did so under a particular set of assumptions: data lived in the cloud, infrastructure was elastic, latency budgets were measured in seconds, and the engine was written in a JVM language because the surrounding ecosystem was JVM.
The third generation is happening now, and is more diffuse. Materialize (2019) showed that incremental view maintenance could be a streaming abstraction in its own right. Arroyo and RisingWave brought SQL-first streaming with column-oriented internals. ClickHouse and Pinot blurred the line between streaming and OLAP. Hyper, Umbra and Velox demonstrated that JIT-compiled query execution could be twenty times faster than interpreted execution. None of these systems is “the” streaming engine; each embodies a different bet about what stream processing should look like in 2025.
NebulaStream is one of those bets. It is an academic project — joint between BIFOLD, the DIMA Group at TU Berlin and the DFKI IAM Group — which means it is both freer to experiment than a production system and more accountable to ideas than to revenue. Its bet is that the shape of computation is changing: data is no longer being produced inside data centres and processed in data centres. It is being produced at the edge — in factories, in vehicles, in medical devices, in agriculture — and the network between the edge and the cloud is the expensive part. A streaming engine that takes that seriously will look different from one that does not.

title: 1  Why Stream Processing? Why Another Engine?
text:
1.2 1.2 What NebulaStream optimises for
The README opens with an unusually clear thesis statement. We will quote it in full because it sets up everything that follows in the book:

NebulaStream is an end-to-end data-management system for cloud-edge-sensor deployments. The platform combines ease of use, extensibility, and efficiency to let teams focus on business logic while the engine optimizes the data path.
We advance this vision through five core technologies:

Heterogeneous Hardware Support — Targets diverse CPU architectures and accelerators such as GPUs and TPUs.
Code Generation — Compiles every query to efficient native code for low latency and energy usage.
In-Network Processing — Pushes operators toward data sources to reduce network traffic.
Adaptive Resource Management — Reacts to topology or workload changes without interrupting queries.


Each of these gets at least one chapter in the book. Two need a brief preview here, because they shape the engine’s design from the very top.
Code generation everywhere. NebulaStream does not interpret a query plan. It compiles the query plan into native machine code, every time, through a tracing-JIT framework called Nautilus that lowers to MLIR and ultimately to LLVM IR. We will see this in detail in Chapter 12. The choice has consequences for almost every other design decision: the operator interface looks more like a producer/consumer protocol than a class hierarchy, intermediate data structures are designed for the JIT (HashMap, PagedVector) rather than the C++ standard library, and the boundary between “query plan” and “executable” is a compile step that can take milliseconds and returns a function pointer. If you have only ever written queries against an interpreter-based engine, this is the single largest mental shift the book will ask you to make.
Cloud-edge-sensor as a first-class deployment target. Almost every streaming engine in production today was designed for the cloud and then asked to run at the edge. The result tends to be a JVM heap on a Raspberry Pi, which is exactly as awkward as it sounds. NebulaStream inverts the question: the edge is the constraint, the cloud is the luxury. C++23, no garbage collector, every byte accounted for. This shows up in the data model (Chapter 3), where the unit of inter-operator data flow is a fixed-size buffer with explicit reference counting, and in the buffer manager (Chapter 4), where pre-allocated pools are the default rather than dynamic allocation. We will see throughout the book how these foundations propagate up the stack.
The other three technologies — heterogeneous hardware, in-network processing, adaptive resource management — are partially implemented and partially aspirational. We will be honest about which parts of the vision are running today and which are research roadmap. The distribution story in particular has moved fast: the coordinator and inter-worker communication that earlier drafts of this book described as “research roadmap” have landed on origin/main since those drafts were written. Chapter 19 covers what shipped and what is still in flight.

text:
1.3 1.3 Why a book on this engine?
There is no shortage of textbooks on databases. Garcia-Molina, Ullman and Widom’s Database Systems: The Complete Book is the canonical undergraduate text on the relational model, SQL, B-trees, transaction processing, and the canonical query optimiser. Petrov’s Database Internals takes the reader on a curated tour of how distributed data systems are actually built — storage engines, consensus, replication. Kleppmann’s Designing Data-Intensive Applications sits one level above: not “how is X implemented” but “how should I think about X.” Akidau, Chernyak and Lax’s Streaming Systems covers the conceptual landscape of stream processing — windowing, triggers, accumulation modes — at a level any practitioner should have in working memory.
Each of these books leaves the same gap. None of them takes a single specimen — a single, concrete, modern stream processing engine — and walks the reader through it end to end. The closest thing is Lions’s Commentary on UNIX 6th Edition, a book written in 1976 that is still in print, because nothing else does for a kernel what Lions did. We need a Lions’s commentary on a stream engine.
NebulaStream is a good specimen for that purpose, for several reasons.
It is small enough to fit in a book: about 876 source files across sixteen modules, mostly C++. Production engines like Flink (about ten times larger) would need three books to cover at this fidelity.
It is modern enough to be interesting: code-generation, MLIR, plugin registries, C++20 concepts, statically-linked plugin systems. Every chapter has something a reader who knows a different engine will not have seen before.
It is documented well enough to be tractable: NebulaStream’s in-tree docs/design/ and docs/technical/ directories contain substantive design documents that explain why a thing works the way it does, not just how. We will lift heavily from them, with attribution, because the team has already done the work of writing down the rationale.
And it is academic enough to be honest about what does not work: production engines bury their workarounds in proprietary commits and internal Slack messages. A research engine can — and does — leave its scars on the surface. Chapter 15’s “the design document says continuation, but the live code uses an unbounded queue” is a microcosm of the kind of intellectual honesty this book is interested in.

title: 1  Why Stream Processing? Why Another Engine?
text:
1.4 1.4 Who is this book for?
Three audiences in roughly decreasing priority:
Graduate students in systems. This book sits at the same “mezzanine” level as Garcia-Molina/Ullman/Widom: between an undergraduate algorithms class and a primary research paper. We assume you can read C++, that you have seen relational algebra, that you know what a watermark is in principle. We do not assume you have built a database. The exercises are designed for self-study and for use in a graduate seminar — none require a problem set in the traditional sense; all point at real tests inside the engine and ask you to run them, observe, and explain.
Engineers building dataflow systems. If you are building Flink operators, Materialize sources, or your own bespoke streaming infrastructure, this book is a tour of one set of choices that you might compare your own choices against. Each chapter ends with a “Real-system reference” sidebar that places NebulaStream’s design next to Flink’s, Spark’s, or Materialize’s. The point is not to claim NebulaStream is better. The point is to make the design space visible.
NebulaStream maintainers and contributors. A book by definition goes stale; a book pinned to a specific commit goes stale fast. But a book that records the reasoning behind a system’s design is a thing the engineers who built that system can hand to a new contributor on their first day. If you are about to send your first PR to NebulaStream, this book is the long form of “go read the design docs” — distilled, cross-referenced, and assembled into a coherent narrative.
What this book is not: a user manual. We will not teach you the SQL you need to express a windowed top-K. The official documentation will. We will use SQL extensively as a vehicle for explaining what the engine does next, but we will not stop to explain what GROUP BY means.

1.5 1.5 What the book does not cover
Three deliberate omissions, each motivated.
Comparative survey. We compare to Flink, Spark, Materialize, Hyper and Arroyo only when a comparison illuminates a NebulaStream design choice, and only in clearly-marked sidebars of half a page or less. If you want a comparative survey of stream processing engines, Akidau, Chernyak and Lax wrote it.
Distributed systems theory. We assume you have at least a working knowledge of leader election, linearisability, network partitions and CAP. Where NebulaStream’s design depends on a specific theoretical result, we cite the paper. We do not re-derive results that other books — Petrov in particular — have already covered in depth.
Anything outside the engine itself. The Kubernetes operator, the deployment scripts, the cloud integration, the observability stack — all useful, none in this book. The line we have drawn is: if it is not under /Users/zeuchste/git/nebulastream/, it is not in scope.

1.7 Summary
NebulaStream is a third-generation streaming engine — academic, C++23-native, JIT-compiled, designed from the start for the cloud- edge-sensor spectrum rather than retrofitted to it. It is small enough to dissect in one book, modern enough to be interesting, and documented well enough to be tractable. The book uses NebulaStream as a single specimen the way an OS textbook uses xv6 or MINIX: not because it is the best engine, but because seeing one engine end to end is more instructive than seeing five engines half-way each.
The remaining 21 chapters fill in the steps between SQL text and running native code, with one chapter per major concern. Chapter 2, next, gives the whirlwind tour: a single query, traced through every module, in about 35 pages.

title: 2  System Tour: From SQL to Native Code
text:
2.1 2.1 Stage 1: SQL → AST → bound logical plan
This chapter is a whirlwind tour. By the end of it you should have a mental picture of every module in the engine, in the right order, and know roughly which chapter to turn to for each. We will not stop to explain anything in detail. We are racing through the pipeline from SQL text to running native code, in about thirty pages, using a single demo query as our chaperone.
The query is the smallest one we can write that exercises the whole stack. It comes from the README:
Three DDL statements declare a source, a physical implementation of that source, and a sink. The fourth statement is the actual query: a trivial projection that copies tuples from demo into result. It has no filter, no join, no window. Anything more complicated would double the length of this chapter without changing the structure of the tour.
We follow that query through seven stages.
Each arrow is one chapter later in the book. Here we will spend about three pages per stage, name the key class and file, and move on.
The text of the query enters the engine through nes-sql-parser/, an ANTLR4-based parser. The grammar lives in nes-sql-parser/AntlrSQL.g4 (about 600 lines). The grammar covers the four DDL/DML shapes we need:
The parser does the syntactic work; it produces an ANTLR parse tree. A second component called the binder converts that tree into a typed LogicalPlan. The binder lives in nes-sql-parser/src/StatementBinder.cpp. Binding is where the engine checks that names resolve, that types make sense, and that the schemas of sources and sinks match the projections in the query. The output of the binder is a LogicalPlan — a typed, validated DAG of operators.
A LogicalPlan is defined in nes-logical-operators/include/Plans/LogicalPlan.hpp. Its core is a vector of root operators and a query identifier:
For our demo query the binder produces a plan with one root: an InlineSinkLogicalOperator named result, whose child is a SourceDescriptorLogicalOperator named demo. A projection node sits between them, but for SELECT value FROM demo INTO result the projection is the identity, so the optimiser will eliminate it shortly.
Chapter 5 covers this stage in full.

2.3 2.3 Stage 3: logical → physical
The optimised logical plan is “what to compute.” The physical plan is “how to compute it.” The conversion happens in nes-query-compiler/, specifically the LowerToPhysicalOperators phase. For our demo query, the lowering chooses:

The source operator becomes a SourcePhysicalOperator that produces TupleBuffers by calling into the FileSource implementation.
The sink becomes a SinkPhysicalOperator that consumes TupleBuffers and forwards them to the FileSink implementation (which uses a CSVOutputFormatter).

The base of the physical operator hierarchy is nes-physical-operators/include/PhysicalOperator.hpp. Like its logical counterpart, it is a C++20 concept rather than a virtual class. Every physical operator implements setup, open, close and execute — the lifecycle methods called during code generation.






TipReal-system reference: how this maps to Flink



Flink also has a logical and physical plan, with similar lowering. The visible difference is that Flink’s physical plan is the input to a Janino-compiled per-operator Java class; NebulaStream’s physical plan is the input to a tracing JIT. Functionally similar; mechanically very different. Chapter 12 covers this gap in detail.


The physical plan for our demo query has two operators with one edge between them. We will look at the physical operator hierarchy in detail in Chapter 10.

title: 2  System Tour: From SQL to Native Code
text:
2.4 2.4 Stage 4: physical plan → pipelined plan
A physical plan is a DAG of operators. A pipelined plan is a DAG of pipelines, where each pipeline is a chain of operators that can be fused into a single tight loop and a single chunk of generated code. Pipeline boundaries occur at operators that cannot be fused through — pipeline breakers — most commonly stateful operators like hash-join builds, aggregations, and window triggers.
The phase that does this is PipeliningPhase, defined in nes-query-compiler/private/Phases/PipeliningPhase.hpp. For our demo query — Source → Sink with no breaker between them — the result is a single pipeline containing both operators.
Pipeline 1: [SourcePhysicalOperator(demo) → SinkPhysicalOperator(result)]
A more interesting query — say SELECT count(*) FROM demo GROUP BY key — would produce two pipelines: one ending at the aggregation build, and one starting at the aggregation probe. We will see the multi-pipeline case in Chapter 11.

title: 2  System Tour: From SQL to Native Code
text:
2.6 2.6 Stage 6: compiled plan → running query
The CompiledQueryPlan is registered with the query engine (nes-query-engine/). Registration causes:

The engine constructs an ExecutableQueryPlan from the CompiledQueryPlan. This adds runtime state — counters, callbacks, per-pipeline operator handlers.
The engine wraps each pipeline in a RunningQueryPlanNode (defined in nes-query-engine/RunningQueryPlan.hpp), which holds a reference count of in-flight WorkTasks and a weak_ptr for safe cross-thread reference.
Sources are wrapped in RunningSource instances (also in nes-query-engine/) and started.

Once running, the engine uses the two-queue scheduler we examined exhaustively in Chapter 15. To recap: sources push TupleBuffers into the bounded admission queue as WorkTasks; worker threads pull from a logical merge of an unbounded internal queue (preferred) and the admission queue (fallback); compiled pipeline functions process buffers and emit follow-up WorkTasks into the unbounded internal queue.
For our demo query, the file source reads demo-input.csv, the CSVInputFormatter parses lines into TupleBuffers, the compiled pipeline projects (in this case, copies) the value field, and the sink’s CSVOutputFormatter writes the values to demo-output.csv. End to end, in production execution mode, this is approximately one function call per tuple, plus the I/O. The compiled code path has the same overhead profile as a hand-written loop with a switch.

2.8 2.8 What we glossed over
We compressed thirty-five pages of careful explanation into one chapter. Most of the compression was honest summarisation. Some of it was outright omission. For the record:

The watermark machinery and the four progress identifiers (OriginId, SequenceNumber, ChunkNumber, Watermark) do not appear in our demo query at all because there is no window. They appear in essentially every other query. Chapter 7 is dedicated to them.
We described JIT compilation in a paragraph. It is the single most consequential design choice in the engine, and Chapter 12 spends its entire length on the tracing approach Nautilus uses.
We did not mention error handling. Every stage above can fail. Chapter 17 covers the ~80 named exception types that NebulaStream defines and how INVARIANT/PRECONDITION macros work alongside them.
We did not mention deployment. The whole tour assumed a single-node worker, because that is what NebulaStream currently fully implements. Chapter 19 is honest about what is and is not yet distributed.

If you read this chapter and found a stage opaque, the corresponding chapter is the cure. If you read this chapter and found nothing opaque, you should probably be reviewing the engine, not reading this book.

text:
2.9 Summary
A NebulaStream query passes through seven stages: parse, bind, optimise, lower, pipeline, compile, run. Each stage is one or two modules. Each transformation is a pure function, except the last, which spawns running threads. The total time from nes-repl accepting the SQL to the first tuple landing in the sink is, for a small query, on the order of milliseconds — most of it spent in the JIT.
The remaining 21 chapters elaborate one stage at a time. By the end of Part IV (Chapter 18), you will have visited every line of code this chapter waved at, in roughly twenty times the depth.

title: 3  Data Model and Type System
text:
3.1 3.1 The type system
Every database has, somewhere near its core, a small set of decisions about what data looks like. What types are first-class? Are tuples mutable? How is a tuple physically laid out in memory? How do operators get them? These decisions, made early, ripple through the rest of the engine.
NebulaStream’s data model is small and deliberate. There are fourteen primitive types and one variable-size escape hatch. Tuples are immutable. The unit of inter-operator data flow is not a tuple but a TupleBuffer — a fixed-size, reference-counted batch of tuples. There is no schema-on-read; every operator knows the schema of every buffer it touches.
This chapter walks through those choices. It is short; the design is, mercifully, simple.
The type system is in nes-data-types/. The core declaration is in nes-data-types/include/DataTypes/DataType.hpp:
Twelve numeric and boolean primitives. One UNDEFINED sentinel. One VARSIZED escape hatch for strings, blobs, and any other variable- length payload.
What is conspicuously absent:
This is a stripped-down, IoT-ready type system. It is also honest: every type maps directly to a C++ type with no impedance mismatch.
Nullability is a property of every field, encoded in a separate enum (NULLABLE) rather than baked into the type. This matches the SQL convention: a UINT64 NOT NULL and a UINT64 (nullable) share the same primitive Type::UINT64. The runtime handles NULL via a separate bitmap; we will see this pattern in Section 3.3.

text:
3.4 3.4 Reference counting and lifetime
TupleBuffer is reference-counted. The reasoning is operational: buffers move freely between threads via the task queue (Chapter 15), and dangling pointers across threads are the kind of bug that takes weeks to track down. Reference counting moves the cost of safety from the programmer to the runtime.
The reference counting is intrusive — the count lives in the controlBlock of the buffer itself, not in a std::shared_ptr header — to avoid the double allocation shared_ptr would otherwise incur. Move steals ownership without bumping the count; copy bumps the count; destruction decrements; reaching zero returns the buffer to its BufferManager.
Buffers can also have child buffers: a VARSIZED payload that overflows the parent buffer’s footprint goes into a child buffer with coupled lifetime. Releasing the parent releases the child. This matters in practice for strings and JSON payloads, where the variable-size content does not fit alongside the fixed-size columns.






TipReal-system reference: Flink’s MemorySegment



Flink’s analogous abstraction is MemorySegment, a fixed-size chunk of memory borrowed from the MemoryManager. The lifetime contract is similar; the implementation differs in two ways. First, Flink’s MemorySegment is not reference-counted — ownership is unique and explicit, in the JVM’s normal sense. Second, Flink supports both heap and off-heap segments transparently. NebulaStream, being a non-JVM language, does not need this distinction: all TupleBuffers come from a pre-allocated native pool.


We will see how BufferManager actually gets these buffers allocated and recycled in the next chapter.

title: 3  Data Model and Type System
section: 3.5 3.5 What you can and cannot mutate
text:
3.5 3.5 What you can and cannot mutate
Tuples inside a buffer are conceptually immutable to operators. An operator that wants to “modify” a tuple — for example, a projection that drops a field — produces a new tuple in a new buffer. The old buffer is unchanged.
This is not pedantic immutability. It enables the engine to do two things that mutable buffers would forbid. First, a buffer can be shared between consumers safely without copy: a fan-out simply hands the same buffer to two downstream operators with the reference count incremented twice. Second, the JIT can be aggressive about read-only assumptions when generating code, since tuples inside buffers really are read-only from the operator’s perspective.
The cost is that operators that look like in-place transformations on paper — Map, Filter — are actually allocate-and-copy in the runtime. The next chapter explains why this is much less expensive than it sounds, given the buffer pool design.

3.6 Summary
NebulaStream’s type system is fourteen primitives plus a variable- size escape, with nullability as a separate per-field flag. Schemas are vectors of fields with $-qualified names supporting source disambiguation. Tuples are immutable from the operator’s perspective and travel in batches inside reference-counted TupleBuffers, which carry the four progress identifiers (OriginId, SequenceNumber, ChunkNumber, Watermark) that the rest of the engine uses to reason about progress. The data model makes deliberate omissions — no nested types, no decimals, no dates — that match the engine’s IoT/edge focus.

title: 4  Buffer Management and Memory Layout
text:
4.1 4.1 The pool: pre-allocated, fixed-size, recycled
The previous chapter introduced the TupleBuffer as the unit of inter-operator data flow. This chapter is about where those buffers come from, where they go, and how they are laid out in memory.
The story is short. NebulaStream uses a pool: a pre-allocated array of fixed-size buffers, recycled with reference counting. Memory layout is a property of each buffer, decided once during optimisation. There is no virtual memory subsystem, no swapping, no buffer-pool replacement policy more sophisticated than “give me a buffer, I’ll give it back.”
The design is austere. The reasons it works are interesting.
The buffer manager lives in nes-memory/include/Runtime/BufferManager.hpp. The defaults reveal the design:
The default configuration: 1024 buffers of 8 KiB each, 64-byte aligned. That is 8 MiB of buffer memory, allocated up front, on worker startup, and not released until shutdown. Buffers are returned to the pool when their reference count drops to zero, not freed individually.
Three things in this design deserve a closer look.
Pre-allocation. Allocating 8 MiB on startup costs one mmap and one zero-fill. Once the engine is warm, no buffer-related allocation occurs on the hot path. This eliminates a class of latency spikes that show up in interpreted-language engines, where garbage collection or first-touch faulting can add milliseconds to an otherwise fast operation. NebulaStream pays the entire memory bill at startup and gets predictable steady-state behaviour in exchange.
Fixed buffer size. Every buffer is 8 KiB. There is no buffer class hierarchy with small buffers and big buffers. Variable-size data — strings, blobs — that does not fit alongside fixed-width columns goes into a child buffer, also from the pool, also 8 KiB, linked into the parent’s lifetime. This means a few common cases waste memory: a VARSIZED field of 100 bytes still takes a full 8 KiB child. The trade-off is operational simplicity: the pool has exactly one slot size, the recycler has exactly one path, and the allocator never has to consult a free-list of differently-sized chunks.
64-byte alignment. Modern x86_64 CPU lines are 64 bytes. Aligning the buffers to a cache-line boundary makes the JIT’s vectorised code much happier; misaligned loads/stores are not free, even on hardware that “supports” them. ARM is similar.

title: 4  Buffer Management and Memory Layout
section: 4.2 4.2 What happens when the pool is empty
text:
4.2 4.2 What happens when the pool is empty
The pool can be exhausted. With 1024 buffers and a query graph of ten operators each holding two buffers in flight, you can support about 50 concurrent worker threads before pressure starts. In practice, the engine sizes the pool to the workload; the default of 1024 is a starting point, not a target.
When the pool is empty, getBufferBlocking does what its name says: it blocks. A worker thread waiting for a buffer is, in effect, backpressured. This is the engine’s third backpressure mechanism, in addition to the source-side admission queue (Chapter 15) and the slow-sink-throttles-source pattern that emerges from the worker thread pool. All three feed into the same end-to-end behaviour: a slow consumer slows down a fast producer.
The non-blocking variant getUnpooledBuffer exists for emergencies — it allocates a fresh buffer outside the pool — but its use is rare and discouraged. The intent is that the pool is the only path.

title: 4  Buffer Management and Memory Layout
text:
4.4 4.4 The MemoryProvider abstraction
A buffer + a layout + a schema is enough information to read and write tuples. NebulaStream wraps these in a MemoryProvider interface that the JIT code uses to access fields. The MemoryProvider knows the layout and produces, for each field access, the correct pointer arithmetic. It is the indirection that makes “row vs. columnar” a per-buffer choice rather than a global choice.
In code-generated terms: when the JIT lowers a Record::read("value"), it asks the MemoryProvider for the address calculation. For a row layout, the address is base + tupleIndex * tupleSize + fieldOffset. For a columnar layout, it is base + fieldOffset * numTuples + tupleIndex * fieldWidth. Both layouts produce code that is nearly as fast as a hand-written loop.
We will see the JIT side of this in Chapter 12.

title: 4  Buffer Management and Memory Layout
text:
4.5 4.5 The pmr escape hatch
The BufferManager::create signature takes a std::pmr::memory_resource. By default it is NesDefaultMemoryAllocator, which calls into the system allocator. The escape hatch is there because workloads on specialised hardware (GPUs, ARM accelerators, persistent-memory devices) may want to allocate buffers from an arena that is not main memory. Plumbing that arena through the standard pmr interface keeps the rest of the engine unchanged.
This is one of the seams where NebulaStream’s “heterogeneous hardware” vision shows up in code: a future GPU backend would provide a pmr::memory_resource that allocates from device memory, and the buffer manager would be unchanged.
crumbs: 4  Buffer Management and Memory Layout

title: 4  Buffer Management and Memory Layout
text:
4.6 Summary
NebulaStream’s buffer manager is a pre-allocated pool of fixed-size (default 8 KiB), 64-byte-aligned, reference-counted buffers distributed via a folly MPMC queue. The design is austere — no size classes, no variable allocations on the hot path, no swap — because the simplification pays for the underlying assumption that the workload fits in main memory. Memory layout (row vs. columnar) is decided per-buffer by an optimiser phase that currently hardcodes row, with the columnar support stubbed in for future work. The pmr::memory_resource extension point allows future hardware backends to provide alternative allocators without touching the rest of the engine.

title: 5  The Query Language and Parser
text:
5.1 5.1 The four DDL/DML shapes
NebulaStream speaks a SQL dialect that is close to standard SQL with two extensions: a way to declare logical and physical sources separately, and INTO clauses that route a query’s output to a named sink. The parser is built on ANTLR4. The binding step turns a parse tree into a typed LogicalPlan. Both live in nes-sql-parser/.
This chapter walks through the language and the parser. The language is not fancy, but the source/sink declaration model deserves a careful look — it is one of the more interesting design choices in the engine.
Every NebulaStream program is built from four kinds of statement. We saw all four in our demo query in Chapter 2. Let us look at each in isolation.
Logical source. Declares a named stream and its schema, with no implementation:
After this statement, demo is a name the rest of the program can refer to, but nothing is producing data yet.
Physical source. Binds an implementation to a logical source:
TYPE selects an implementation from the source registry. The SET(…) clause carries arbitrary key-value configuration. The backticks around SOURCE and TYPE are SQL-standard escaping for identifiers that collide with reserved words.
Sink. Declares an output channel with a schema and an implementation:
Note that sinks combine the logical declaration and the physical implementation in one statement, unlike sources. We will see why in Section 5.2.
Query. A familiar SELECT with one twist: the output is named:
INTO result is required; NebulaStream queries always produce a named output, never an anonymous result set. There is no client- side cursor; if you want results in nes-repl, you declare a PrintSink and route the query into it.

title: 5  The Query Language and Parser
crumbs: 5  The Query Language and Parser

title: 5  The Query Language and Parser
text:
5.2 5.2 Why two source statements?
The split between logical and physical source declarations is the non-obvious part of the language. Most SQL engines combine the two: CREATE TABLE foo (x INT) ENGINE=File LOCATION='/path' or its moral equivalent. NebulaStream separates them. Why?
The reason is that one logical source can have multiple physical sources, and the engine treats them as a single logical input. A fleet of 200 vehicles can each have its own physical source — perhaps an MQTT topic per vehicle — that all feed a single logical source named vehicles. A query that reads from vehicles reads from the union of all 200 physical sources, with the engine managing parallelism, watermarks, and per-physical-source state under the hood.






NoteExample 5.1: a fleet of vehicles



CREATE LOGICAL SOURCE vehicles(
    id UINT64,
    speed FLOAT64,
    creationTS UINT64);

CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE FOR vehicles TYPE TCP
    SET('vehicle-1.local' AS HOST, '5001' AS PORT, ...);
CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE FOR vehicles TYPE TCP
    SET('vehicle-2.local' AS HOST, '5001' AS PORT, ...);
-- ... 198 more ...
CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE FOR vehicles TYPE TCP
    SET('vehicle-200.local' AS HOST, '5001' AS PORT, ...);

SELECT id, speed FROM vehicles WHERE speed > 100 INTO alerts;
The SELECT is unaware of the 200-physical fan-in. The engine treats vehicles as a single logical input whose physical realisation happens to be 200 TCP connections. Adding or removing a vehicle is a CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE or its inverse — no query edit required.


Sinks do not need this split because the analogous fan-out is handled differently — typically by the application code that consumes from the sink, not by the engine. A future direction may introduce a logical/physical sink split if the symmetry becomes useful; today it does not.

title: 5  The Query Language and Parser
text:
5.3 5.3 The grammar
The grammar lives in nes-sql-parser/AntlrSQL.g4. Here is the relevant slice:
// nes-sql-parser/AntlrSQL.g4
createLogicalSourceDefinition:
    LOGICAL SOURCE sourceName=identifier schemaDefinition fromQuery?;

createPhysicalSourceDefinition:
    PHYSICAL SOURCE FOR logicalSource=identifier
    TYPE type=identifier
    optionsClause?;

createSinkDefinition:
    SINK sinkName=identifier schemaDefinition
    TYPE type=identifier optionsClause?;

optionsClause: (SET '(' options=namedConfigExpressionSeq ')');
Three observations.
First, the grammar is small. NebulaStream’s SQL is intentionally a subset of standard SQL; you will not find WITH RECURSIVE, correlated subqueries, or PIVOT here. The streaming workloads the engine targets simply do not need them.
Second, the grammar is unambiguous about TYPE. Both physical source and sink declarations have a TYPE clause that selects the implementation by name. The name must match an entry in the source/sink registry (Chapter 13); unknown types produce a binding error.
Third, the optional fromQuery on createLogicalSourceDefinition hints at a feature the grammar supports: a logical source can be defined as the result of a query over other sources. This is NebulaStream’s analogue of a materialised view. We will not cover it in this chapter — it is a small slice — but it exists.

section: 5.5 5.5 The query catalog and source catalog
text:
5.5 5.5 The query catalog and source catalog
Two pieces of state outlive any single query: the SourceCatalog and the SinkCatalog. Both live in nes-sources/include/Sources/SourceCatalog.hpp and the analogous sink path. They are simple key-to-descriptor maps.
When CREATE LOGICAL SOURCE demo(value UINT64) runs, the catalog gets a new entry. When CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE FOR demo … runs, the catalog gets a physical descriptor attached to the existing logical entry. When the user submits SELECT … FROM demo, the binder looks up demo in the catalog to resolve the schema and attach the physical descriptors.
Catalog entries persist across queries within a single worker process. They do not (yet) persist across worker restarts. This is a deliberate choice: NebulaStream is not, today, designed as a metadata store.

title: 5  The Query Language and Parser
text:
5.6 Summary
NebulaStream’s SQL dialect uses four statement shapes: logical source, physical source, sink, and query. The split between logical and physical sources is the most distinctive feature: a single logical source can have many physical realisations, and the engine treats them as one fan-in stream. The grammar is small and ANTLR4-based; binding produces a typed LogicalPlan from the parse tree by resolving names against a SourceCatalog, type- checking expressions, and assembling a DAG of LogicalOperators. There is no Calcite-scale validator; the language is small enough for a straightforward visitor.

title: 6  Logical Operator Algebra
text:
6.1 6.1 The operator family
A logical plan is what the engine has decided your query means, expressed as a directed acyclic graph of operators. Each operator declares its inputs and its output. The graph is the engine’s internal language for “what to compute”; everything from optimisation through code generation operates on it.
This chapter walks through the operator vocabulary, the structural properties of the graph (immutable, type-erased, schema-annotated), and the conventions that recur in later parts of the book.
Every logical operator in NebulaStream lives in nes-logical-operators/include/Operators/. The full list as of the pinned commit:
Eight operators. Notably absent:
This minimalism is, again, intentional. Streaming queries are shallow; complicating the algebra adds optimiser surface without adding meaningful workloads.

title: 6  Logical Operator Algebra
6  Logical Operator Algebra
text:
6.5 6.5 The trait set: optimiser scratchpad
Each operator carries a trait set — a set of decorations that optimiser passes attach to record decisions. Examples:

JoinImplementationTypeTrait — set by DecideJoinTypesRule, records whether the join should be a hash join or a nested-loop join.
MemoryLayoutTrait — set by DecideMemoryLayoutRule, records the chosen row/columnar layout.
OriginIdTrait — set by OriginIdInferenceRule, records the origin identifier of the operator’s output.

Traits are a generic mechanism. Each trait is a class; an operator holds a TraitSet (essentially a typed map) and exposes getTrait<T>() to retrieve a specific trait if present. Traits are how optimiser passes communicate downstream without baking decisions into operator constructors.
We will see traits used extensively in Chapter 9 (rule-based optimisation) and Chapter 10 (physical lowering).

title: 6  Logical Operator Algebra
text:
6.6 6.6 Reading a plan
A LogicalPlan has an explain() method that produces a textual representation, useful for debugging and tests. The output is indented to show the tree structure:
SinkLogicalOperator(name=alerts, schema={vehicles$key: UINT64, avgSpeed: FLOAT64})
└── WindowedAggregationLogicalOperator(window=Tumbling(1s), groupingKey=[vehicles$key], aggregations=[Avg(vehicles$speed)])
    └── SourceDescriptorLogicalOperator(name=vehicles, schema={…})
Most systests assert on this textual representation. If you change an operator’s schema or its trait set, the explain string changes, and a test failure tells you something visible has shifted.

title: 6  Logical Operator Algebra
text:
6.7 Summary
NebulaStream’s logical algebra is small (eight operators), built on C++20 concepts rather than virtual inheritance, immutable (a transformation produces a new plan), and decorated by an optimiser- extensible trait set. Stateful operators carry extra metadata — window type, grouping key, aggregation functions — and create new origins so downstream operators can reason about their watermarks independently. The minimalism of the algebra is matched by the minimalism of the optimiser (Chapter 9), and the immutability is matched by the pure-function style of the optimiser phases.

title: 7  Time, Watermarks, and Progress
text:
7.1 7.1 Two clocks: event time and processing time
If a streaming engine has only one hard problem, it is this one. When can I close a window?
A batch system can close a window because the data is finite: the input file ends, the partition is complete, the day is over. A streaming system cannot. Tuples can arrive out of order, sources can fall behind, the network can hiccup, and a tuple from “ten seconds ago” can show up after a tuple from “five seconds ago.” The engine has to commit to closing a window at some point — otherwise it never produces a result — but committing too early loses data, and committing too late builds an unbounded backlog.
Watermarks are the answer the streaming community has converged on (Akidau et al. 2015). A watermark is a promise: “no event with a timestamp before t will arrive from this stream after this point.” When all upstream operators have promised a watermark beyond t, the engine can safely close all windows that end at t.
NebulaStream implements this with a four-tuple of identifiers attached to every TupleBuffer: OriginId, SequenceNumber, ChunkNumber, and Watermark. Three of the four are not timestamps. They exist because watermarks alone are not enough.
This is one of the longest chapters in the book. The mechanism is intricate, and getting it wrong produces silently incorrect results — the worst kind of bug.
Every tuple has, at least conceptually, two timestamps.
Event time. When the event happened in the real world. A vehicle sensor records its speed at 10:00:00.123. The tuple representing that reading carries 10:00:00.123 as its event-time timestamp.
Processing time. When the engine processed the tuple. The tuple might arrive at the sensor’s TCP source at 10:00:00.456, get parsed and forwarded at 10:00:00.500, and reach a downstream operator at 10:00:00.600. Each is a different processing-time timestamp.
A query like SELECT AVG(speed) GROUP BY vehicle WINDOW TUMBLING(1 SECOND) is ambiguous unless you say which clock the window applies to. NebulaStream defaults to event time when a field is named (WINDOW TUMBLING(creationTS, SIZE 1 SEC)) and ingestion time (the source’s processing-time stamp at ingest) when no field is named.
Event-time windows are the interesting case. They are deterministic across replays — re-running the same input produces the same window contents — but they require watermarks to know when to fire. Processing-time windows are easy to fire (the local clock decides) but non-deterministic. Streaming engineers prefer event-time windows almost always (Akidau et al. 2018); this is what we will focus on.

title: 7  Time, Watermarks, and Progress
text:
7.2 7.2 The four progress identifiers
Every TupleBuffer in NebulaStream carries four identifiers that together determine its position in the engine’s progress lattice. They are defined in nes-common/include/Identifiers/Identifiers.hpp:
// nes-common/include/Identifiers/Identifiers.hpp
using OriginId = NESStrongType<uint64_t, struct OriginId_, 0, 1>;
using SequenceNumber = NESStrongType<uint64_t, struct SequenceNumber_, 0, 1>;
using ChunkNumber = NESStrongType<uint64_t, struct ChunkNumber_,
                                  SequenceNumber::INVALID,
                                  SequenceNumber::INITIAL>;
(Watermark is a uint64_t carrying the event-time stamp.)
Why four, not just one? Each addresses a different mode of failure:
OriginId: which stream is this from? A query joining two streams has tuples from two origins; the engine needs to track their watermarks separately, then take the minimum to advance the join’s notion of progress. A WindowedAggregation produces a new origin for its output. Without distinct origin identifiers, the engine cannot reason about per-source progress.
SequenceNumber: which logical batch is this? A source produces an ordered sequence of logical events. The sequence number is strictly monotonic, per origin. It is the engine’s primary ordering key; gaps in the sequence indicate missing data.
ChunkNumber: which physical buffer within the batch? A single logical event from a source may not fit in one buffer. A JSON record of 12 KiB exceeds the default 8 KiB buffer; it produces two physical buffers, both with the same SequenceNumber but different ChunkNumbers. The chunk number disambiguates them and records whether more chunks are coming.
Watermark: how far has time advanced? The event-time stamp beyond which no earlier-event-time tuple is expected. Chunked correctly, this is the engine’s key for closing windows.






NoteExample 7.1: a single buffer’s progress 4-tuple



A buffer freshly emitted by a TCP source might carry:
OriginId       = 7        # the seventh logical source
SequenceNumber = 152       # 152nd batch from this source
ChunkNumber    = 0        # first (and only) chunk of this batch
Watermark      = 1715000000000  # nanoseconds since epoch
isLastChunk    = true     # no more chunks for this sequence
A window operator reading this buffer learns: from origin 7, the 152nd batch has arrived in full, with no event-time stamp earlier than 1715000000000 expected from this source.

title: 7  Time, Watermarks, and Progress
7  Time, Watermarks, and Progress
section: 7.4 7.4 Why sequence numbers matter for windows
text:
7.4 7.4 Why sequence numbers matter for windows
Watermarks alone are not enough to close a window correctly. The problem is that watermarks are a promise about the future, not the past. A window that should fire at watermark 1000 cannot fire just because some buffer arrived with watermark 1100; the engine needs to know that all the buffers with event times below 1000 have arrived.
This is where sequence numbers carry their weight. Sources commit not only to a watermark but to a contiguous sequence of buffers. If the source has emitted buffers with sequence numbers 0, 1, 2, 4 (note: 3 is missing), the engine cannot close a window even if the watermark on buffer 4 says “everything before 1000 is here.” Buffer 3 has not yet arrived; until it does, the window is incomplete.
The engine therefore tracks, per origin, the highest contiguous sequence number it has seen. Watermarks advance only as far as the contiguous prefix allows. A non-contiguous gap stalls progress. This is the engine’s principal correctness mechanism: it prefers to halt rather than fire a window with missing data.






NoteExample 7.2: a missing sequence number



Source emits buffers with sequence numbers 100, 101, 102, then 104. Watermarks 100, 200, 300, 500. The engine’s per-origin state is:
contiguousPrefix = 102   # 103 is missing
maxSeenSequence  = 104
maxSeenWatermark = 500
effectiveWatermark = 300  # the watermark on contiguous prefix
A window that ends at event time 250 can fire (250 < 300). A window that ends at event time 400 cannot — even though the maxSeenWatermark is 500, sequence 103 might carry a tuple with event time 350. The engine waits.
When sequence 103 arrives (with watermark, say, 400), the contiguous prefix advances to 104, the effective watermark advances to 500, and the window ending at 400 fires.

title: 7  Time, Watermarks, and Progress
7  Time, Watermarks, and Progress
text:
7.6 7.6 Window types
NebulaStream’s window operators support three classical window shapes:
Tumbling. Fixed-size, non-overlapping. WINDOW TUMBLING(ts, SIZE 1 SEC) produces non-overlapping 1-second buckets. Each tuple belongs to exactly one window.
Sliding. Fixed-size, overlapping. WINDOW SLIDING(ts, SIZE 5 SEC, ADVANCE 1 SEC) produces overlapping 5-second windows that advance every 1 second. Each tuple belongs to up to five windows.
Session. Variable-size, gap-defined. A session window groups tuples whose timestamps are within gap of one another. Used for “all events from a single user’s browsing session.”
The window-type hierarchy is in nes-logical-operators/include/WindowTypes/Types/. Each window type knows how to compute, for a given event-time stamp, the set of windows that contain that timestamp.

title: 7  Time, Watermarks, and Progress
text:
7.7 7.7 The build/probe split
A windowed aggregation lowers, physically, into a build phase that accumulates state and a probe phase that emits results when windows close. The build phase is keyed on the grouping key plus the window identity; it maintains a hash map of partial results. The probe phase is triggered by watermark advancement: when the engine’s notion of progress crosses a window’s end timestamp, the probe walks the hash map and emits one tuple per window.
The physical operators are in nes-physical-operators/include/: WindowBuildPhysicalOperator and WindowProbePhysicalOperator. A WindowBasedOperatorHandler (nes-physical-operators/include/WindowBasedOperatorHandler.hpp) coordinates the two: it owns the slice store, the watermark processors (one for build, one for probe), and the trigger logic.






TipReal-system reference: how Flink does this



Flink uses a similar build/probe split, with watermarks driving window firing. The two important differences are:

Flink stores window state in RocksDB by default, not in memory. NebulaStream is in-memory only (Chapter 16). For workloads that exceed memory, NebulaStream relies on the operator developer to spill manually; Flink handles it transparently with state backends.
Flink uses a single watermark per parallel operator instance, tracking progress through that instance’s view of the world. NebulaStream uses a per-origin watermark, allowing more precise reasoning about multi-source joins. The trade-off is bookkeeping complexity.

title: 7  Time, Watermarks, and Progress
text:
7.8 7.8 Watermarks across workers
So far this chapter has described watermark propagation as if the whole query ran in one process. In a distributed deployment (Chapter 19), the operator graph spans workers, and watermarks have to cross the wire.
The four-tuple progress identifiers we have been discussing — OriginId, SequenceNumber, ChunkNumber, Watermark — are exactly what makes this work cleanly. The information that matters at a network boundary is what an upstream origin has promised, not which thread is processing what. Promises travel as TupleBuffer metadata.
When a NetworkSink (Chapter 19) ships a buffer over to a NetworkSource on another worker, the buffer’s metadata — including the four progress identifiers — travels with it. The receiving side does not invent new origin or sequence numbers; it forwards the originating ones. A downstream operator on the receiving worker sees the same OriginId it would have seen if the whole query were single-node. The engine’s notion of progress is consistent across the boundary.
The implication: a join on worker B between an origin from worker A and a local origin behaves correctly because the MultiOriginWatermarkProcessor on worker B sees both origins’ watermarks — the local one directly, the remote one via the NetworkSource — and takes the minimum. The minimum-of-origins discipline that holds within one worker holds across many.
What does not travel automatically is trust. If worker A is unreachable (network partition), the receiving side cannot distinguish “A is slow and will catch up” from “A has crashed and will never catch up.” The engine’s current behaviour is conservative: a watermark that has not advanced is held to be not-yet-advanced, and downstream windows wait. Chapter 22 discusses adaptive timeout policies as future work.






NoteExample 7.4: a windowed aggregation across workers



A query reading from two sensors (sensor-A on worker A, sensor-B on worker B) and aggregating into one-second windows on worker C:
worker A: source(sensor-A) → NetworkSink(channel-1)
                                            │
worker B: source(sensor-B) → NetworkSink(channel-2)
                                            │
                                            ▼
worker C: NetworkSource×2 → AggregationBuild → AggregationProbe → sink
Two OriginIds flow into worker C’s aggregation. The MultiOriginWatermarkProcessor on the build side sees both; the aggregation does not fire windows until both origins’ watermarks have crossed the window’s end. If worker A’s network briefly hiccups, worker C waits — windows from before the hiccup eventually fire when the buffers catch up; windows that depend on data that never arrives stall conservatively.

title: 7  Time, Watermarks, and Progress
section: 7.9 7.9 Garbage collection: when state can be released
text:
7.9 7.9 Garbage collection: when state can be released
A window’s state — the partial aggregation hash map keyed on (window-id, group-key) — has to be released eventually, or the engine grows without bound.
NebulaStream uses a slice abstraction: state is partitioned into slices keyed on a contiguous time range, and a slice can be released once the engine’s watermark has advanced past the slice’s end. The garbage collector (garbageCollectSlicesAndWindows on the WindowBasedOperatorHandler) walks slices on every probe pass and deallocates those that are guaranteed to never receive late tuples.
The decision is conservative: a slice is released only when all upstream watermarks have passed it. Out-of-order tuples that arrive after release are dropped silently. NebulaStream does not, today, support late-data side outputs the way Flink does.

title: 7  Time, Watermarks, and Progress
text:
7.10 Summary
NebulaStream tracks progress with a four-tuple per TupleBuffer: OriginId distinguishes streams, SequenceNumber orders batches per origin, ChunkNumber distinguishes physical buffers belonging to the same logical batch, and Watermark carries the event-time promise. Watermarks advance through the operator graph by minimum-of-input, gated by the contiguous sequence-number prefix to ensure no missing batch is masked by a later watermark. Multi-chunk events are reassembled by the SequenceShredder. Window operators split into build and probe phases, with watermarks triggering probe and slice-based garbage collection releasing closed-window state. The mechanism is intricate but conservative: when in doubt, the engine waits.

title: 8  Sources, Sinks, and Input Formatters
text:
8.1 8.1 The source contract
A stream processing engine without sources is just an interpreter for a query language. NebulaStream’s source and sink subsystem is what makes the engine plug into the world — into files, into TCP streams, into Kafka, into whatever the data is actually flowing through.
The subsystem has four moving parts: sources (where bytes come from), sinks (where bytes go to), input formatters (how bytes become tuples) and output formatters (how tuples become bytes). Each is plugin-extensible through a static registry; the engine shipping today supports a handful of formats out of the box and a handful more as optional plugins.
This chapter walks through all four parts, with attention to two non-obvious design choices: the strict separation between source and formatter, and the fully-specified descriptor model that lets workers run sources without coordinator round-trips.
A source’s job is to fill a TupleBuffer with raw bytes. The contract is in nes-sources/include/Sources/Source.hpp:
One method: fillTupleBuffer. The buffer is given to the source empty; the source writes raw bytes into it and returns either “end of stream” or “I wrote N bytes.” That is it.
What this contract does not do: the source does not parse the bytes. A CSV source produces a buffer full of newline-separated ASCII; a JSON source produces a buffer full of brace-bracketed JSON text. Neither knows what the schema is. Parsing happens later.
The reason for this separation is throughput. Reading from a TCP socket and parsing CSV are different work; doing them in different threads (or, more importantly, on different cores) lets each one saturate its bottleneck independently. The source thread’s bottleneck is I/O; the formatter thread’s bottleneck is CPU. They should not block each other.

8.4 8.4 SequenceShredder: tuples that span buffers
A 12 KiB JSON record does not fit in an 8 KiB raw buffer. A 100-line CSV file followed by a partial 101st line at byte 8190 leaves the 101st line straddling buffer boundary. The formatter has to handle these cases.
The component that does is the SequenceShredder, documented extensively in nes-input-formatters/README.md. The shredder maintains per-source state about partial tuples and reassembles them when the missing pieces arrive. It is what allows the formatter to operate on independent buffers in parallel without losing tuples that cross boundaries.
The shredder is the reason tuples carry SequenceNumber and ChunkNumber (Chapter 7): chunks let the shredder know that sequence number S has multiple physical pieces.

8.6 8.6 The plugin registry
Sources, sinks, input formatters and output formatters are all plugin-registered. The CMake macro add_plugin registers an internal plugin; add_plugin_as_library registers an optional one. Activating an optional plugin is a single line in nes-plugins/CMakeLists.txt:
// nes-plugins/CMakeLists.txt
activate_optional_plugin("Sources/TCPSource" ON)

activate_optional_plugin("InputFormatters/JSONInputFormatter" ON)

TipReal-system reference: how Telegraf does this



Telegraf, the InfluxData metrics agent, has 300+ source plugins (“inputs” in their terminology), each compiled into the binary through a similar register-by-name pattern. NebulaStream’s plugin system is small in comparison (a dozen sources today) but architecturally the same.
The interesting technical difference is that Telegraf’s plugins are Go interfaces with dynamic dispatch, whereas NebulaStream’s are C++ types resolved at compile time. NebulaStream pays for static linking with a slower build but a faster runtime.

NebulaStream’s source and sink subsystem separates I/O (sources, sinks) from format conversion (formatters), with each part plugin-extensible through a static registry. title: 9  Rule-Based Logical Optimization
text:
9.1 9.1 The five rules
The optimiser sits between the parser and the code generator. Its job is to rewrite a logical plan into a better one. “Better” can mean many things — fewer joins, smaller intermediate results, plans that parallelise more naturally — but in NebulaStream it means something quite specific.
NebulaStream’s optimiser is rule-based: it applies a fixed sequence of transformations, each a pure function from plan to plan. There is no cost model, no plan-space exploration, no estimation of cardinalities. Every query gets the same five rules applied in the same order. The system Volcano (Graefe 1994) would have called such a thing a “preprocessor” rather than an optimiser.
This chapter walks through that preprocessor. We will not pretend it is more sophisticated than it is. The interesting part is not the rules themselves — they are simple — but why the engine chose simplicity here.
The entry point is QueryOptimizer::optimize, in nes-query-optimizer/src/QueryOptimizer.cpp. We saw it in Chapter 2:
Five rules, applied in order. The order matters — let us go through them.
1. RedundantProjectionRemoval. A projection that selects every field of its input in input order is a no-op. If the binder produced one (and it often does, for the SELECT * shape), this rule deletes it.
2. RedundantUnionRemoval. A union with one input is just that input. Eliminate the union node.
3. TypeInference. Walk the plan and annotate every operator with its input and output schema. This rule does not transform the plan structurally; it decorates it. Subsequent rules and the lowering phase rely on these annotations.
4. DecideJoinTypes. For each join in the plan, choose between hash join, nested-loop join, and any future join implementation. This is the most logically complex rule; we examine it in Section 9.3.
5. DecideMemoryLayout. Choose row vs. columnar layout for each operator’s output. Currently always row (Chapter 4); the infrastructure exists for future per-operator decisions.
That is all. No predicate pushdown. No projection pushdown. No join reordering. No common-subexpression elimination. The optimiser has no opinion on those questions.

title: 9  Rule-Based Logical Optimization
9  Rule-Based Logical Optimization
text:
9.2 9.2 Why no cost-based optimisation?
Most relational databases have a cost-based optimiser. They have one because a join over a billion rows of customers and a million rows of orders can have wildly different costs depending on which side is the build, whether indexes apply, and what predicates can be pushed down. The optimiser’s job is to navigate that combinatorial space.
NebulaStream’s workloads typically do not look like that. A streaming query is small (tens of operators, not hundreds), shallow (rarely more than two joins), and bounded in fan-out (the schemas of streaming sources are usually narrow). The space the optimiser would need to navigate is small enough that the right plan is mostly the obvious plan.
There are also two specifically streaming reasons. First, statistics are hard to maintain over an unbounded input — the cardinality estimate for “the number of vehicles” is a moving target. Second, the cost of a wrong plan is amortised over the query’s runtime; a streaming query running for a month will eventually pay back any one-time optimisation overhead, but it will not benefit from the optimiser re-considering after the workload shifts (and re-considering during operation is its own problem, as Chapter 22 discusses).
The pragmatic conclusion is that a rule-based preprocessor is sufficient for this engine, today. As NebulaStream takes on larger queries — multi-join analytical streams over many heterogeneous sources — that conclusion may need to be revisited.






TipReal-system reference: when CBO matters



PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server invest heavily in cost-based optimisation because their workloads include OLAP queries with five-way joins and complex predicates. Apache Calcite provides a CBO framework that Flink uses for its SQL surface.
Materialize uses no traditional CBO either, for similar reasons to NebulaStream: streaming queries have less plan-space to search, and the cost of a wrong plan is amortised. Hyper and Umbra do CBO at runtime, recompiling when the cost model says a better plan exists. NebulaStream sits at the simpler end of this spectrum.

title: 9  Rule-Based Logical Optimization
9  Rule-Based Logical Optimization
text:
9.4 9.4 Static vs. semantic rules
The rules in nes-query-optimizer/include/Rules/Static/ are pure syntactic rewrites: they look at the plan structure and rewrite it. They do not need to consult any external state. The five rules called by QueryOptimizer::optimize are static rules.
There is also a directory nes-query-optimizer/include/Rules/Semantic/ containing rules like TypeInferenceRule, SourceInferenceRule, SinkBindingRule, OriginIdInferenceRule. These are typically called inside the binder (Chapter 5) rather than the optimiser proper, because they consult the source/sink catalog and the schema of catalog-resolved sources. The distinction is more historical than principled — both are plan-to-plan transformations — but it shows up in the directory layout.
For our purposes, both kinds are “rules”: pure functions that transform the plan.

title: 9  Rule-Based Logical Optimization
text:
9.5 9.5 The trait set, revisited
We met the trait set in Chapter 6. Optimiser rules are the principal users. Each rule attaches a trait to the operators it touches, recording the decision the rule made:



Rule
Trait it attaches




TypeInference
input/output schema annotations


OriginIdInference
OriginIdTrait per stateful operator


DecideJoinTypes
JoinImplementationTypeTrait


DecideMemoryLayout
MemoryLayoutTrait



Downstream — particularly in the lowering phase (Chapter 10) — the lowering rules read these traits to decide which physical operator to instantiate. Hash-join build vs. nested-loop build is one read of the join trait.
The trait pattern is what makes the optimiser composable. Each rule is independent of the others; they communicate through traits rather than through implicit structure. Adding a new rule that attaches a new trait does not invalidate existing rules.

title: 9  Rule-Based Logical Optimization
text:
9.6 Summary
NebulaStream’s optimiser is a fixed sequence of five rules, applied in order, each a pure function. There is no cost-based optimisation, no plan-space exploration, and no statistics — a deliberate choice matching the engine’s typical workload of small, shallow streaming queries. The most non-trivial rule, DecideJoinTypes, makes a structural rather than statistical decision: hash join if the predicate is an equi-join, nested-loop otherwise. Rules communicate their decisions through a trait set attached to operators, which the lowering phase (Chapter 10) reads to choose physical implementations.

title: 10  Physical Lowering and Operator Choice
text:
10.1 10.1 The physical operator concept
A logical operator says what to compute. A physical operator says how. The distinction matters because there is usually more than one way: a join can be hash or nested-loop; an aggregation can be key-grouped or globally streamed; a memory layout can be row or columnar. Lowering is the engine’s commitment to a particular how.
In NebulaStream, lowering is a phase in nes-query-compiler/ called LowerToPhysicalOperators. It runs after optimisation and before pipelining. By the time it finishes, every logical operator has been replaced by an instance of a physical operator class that knows how to participate in code generation.
Physical operators, like logical operators, are defined through a C++20 concept rather than a class hierarchy. The concept lives in nes-physical-operators/include/PhysicalOperator.hpp:
Four lifecycle methods, executed during code generation:
These look like a standard producer/consumer protocol because they are. NebulaStream’s physical operators are essentially Volcano- style operators with the per-tuple next() replaced by a per-batch execute(Record) and the whole protocol expressed at code- generation time rather than at runtime.

10.5 10.5 Aggregation: same structure, different state
Aggregations also lower into a build/probe pair. The build inserts records into a hash map keyed on the grouping key (or, for global aggregations, into a single accumulator). The probe walks the hash map after each window fires and emits one record per group.
The interesting difference from joins is that the aggregation’s hash map values are partial aggregates, not records. For AVG(speed), the value is (sum, count); for MAX(value) it is the running maximum. The aggregation function knows how to combine a partial aggregate with an incoming value (the combine step) and how to convert a partial aggregate into a result tuple (the extract step).
The actual aggregation classes are in nes-physical-operators/include/Aggregation/. The aggregation function vocabulary is in nes-logical-operators/include/Operators/Windows/Aggregations/ — SUM, COUNT, MIN, MAX, AVG, plus a generic UDF aggregation slot.

10.6 10.6 What is not in the lowering phase
Several decisions feel like they ought to belong here but do not.
Code generation belongs to the next two phases (pipelining, then JIT). The lowering phase produces physical operator objects; it does not generate any code. The objects expose methods that the JIT calls.
Memory allocation belongs to setup-time bookkeeping in the runtime, driven by physical operators but not allocated by the lowering rules. The lowering rule says “this build operator will need a hash map of size approximately N”; the runtime allocates when the query starts.
Parallelism decisions also do not happen here. Whether to parallelise the join across multiple worker threads is decided at runtime by the task scheduler (Chapter 15), not at lowering time.
The lowering phase’s scope is narrow: pick a class, instantiate it with the right configuration, hand it to the next phase.

The lowering phase rewrites a logical plan into a physical plan by replacing each logical operator with one or more physical operators. title: 11  Pipelining and Compiled Plans
text:
11.1 11.1 The shape of a pipeline
A physical plan is a DAG of operators. A pipelined plan is a DAG of pipelines, each pipeline being a chain of operators that the JIT can fuse into a single tight loop. Pipelining is the engine’s answer to a question every query compiler eventually faces: where do I draw the boundaries of the generated code?
The wrong answer in either direction is bad. Generate one giant function for the whole plan and you waste compile time on code that does not need to be co-optimised, and you cannot release intermediate state until the whole query finishes. Generate one function per operator and you incur a function-call boundary at every record, defeating the point of code generation in the first place.
The right answer is well known (Neumann 2011): fuse what can be fused (operators that pass records one-at-a-time), break at operators that materialise (joins, aggregations, sorts). The operators where you must break are called pipeline breakers.
NebulaStream’s PipeliningPhase does exactly this.
A pipeline is a sequence of physical operators with a single producer (a source operator or a probe operator) and a single consumer (a sink operator or a build operator). Records flow from producer to consumer through the chain, one at a time, with no intermediate materialisation. The JIT generates one function whose loop body executes the chain.
The data structure is in nes-query-compiler/include/PipelinedQueryPlan.hpp:
A PipelinedQueryPlan is a vector of Pipelines, distinguishing the source pipelines (those starting at a source operator) from the rest. The distinction matters because source pipelines are the ones that get scheduled when sources produce data; everything else is reactive.

text:
11.2 11.2 The pipelining phase
The phase is PipeliningPhase, in nes-query-compiler/private/Phases/PipeliningPhase.hpp. Its algorithm, simplified:

Walk the physical plan in topological order.
For each operator, decide whether to continue the current pipeline or start a new pipeline.
The decision is encoded as PipelinePolicy::Continue or PipelinePolicy::ForceNew.

The enum and its case analysis live in nes-query-compiler/src/Phases/PipeliningPhase.cpp:
// nes-query-compiler/src/Phases/PipeliningPhase.cpp
enum class PipelinePolicy : uint8_t {
    Continue,   /// Uses the current pipeline for the next operator
    ForceNew    /// Enforces a new pipeline for the next operator
};
The recursive builder applies five rules in order; the first match wins:









#

Why

2

Rule 4 is the override that catches operators that would have been fusible but cannot be because two upstream pipelines feed them. The check is a single line:
// nes-query-compiler/src/Phases/PipeliningPhase.cpp (sketch)
if (policy != PipelinePolicy::ForceNew && mergePoints.contains(opId)) {
    policy = PipelinePolicy::ForceNew;
}
A sink is always a pipeline breaker because the engine does not fuse sink writes with operator computation. A stateful build (join build, aggregation build) is a pipeline breaker because the build materialises into a hash map. A stateful probe is the start of a new pipeline, because it consumes from the materialised state asynchronously.
The fusible operators — Selection, Projection, Map — get PipelinePolicy::Continue by default and become part of whatever pipeline they sit in.

title: 11  Pipelining and Compiled Plans
text:
11.3 11.3 Pipeline breakers, walked through
For our running demo query (Chapter 2), the pipelined plan is trivial:
Pipeline 1: [SourcePhysicalOperator(demo) → SinkPhysicalOperator(result)]
One source pipeline, one sink, no break in between (because there is no stateful operator). The JIT generates one function for the whole pipeline; the loop body reads a record from the source, projects (in this case, identity), writes to the sink. Done.
For a hash-join query, the picture is more interesting. Consider:
SELECT * FROM r JOIN s ON r.key = s.key INTO matched;
After lowering (Chapter 10), the physical plan is:
Sink ← HJProbe ← Source(s)
       HJBuild ← Source(r)
HJProbe is the consumer of records from s; HJBuild is the consumer of records from r. The two halves share an OperatorHandlerId that points to a single hash map.
After pipelining, this becomes three pipelines:
Pipeline A (source pipeline): [Source(r) → HJBuild]
Pipeline B (source pipeline): [Source(s) → HJProbe → Sink]
HJBuild is a pipeline breaker; pipeline A ends at it. HJProbe starts pipeline B. The two pipelines are independent at the scheduler’s level — they run as separate compiled functions, each producing/consuming WorkTasks — but they communicate through the shared hash map handler.






NoteExample 11.1: aggregation pipelines



A windowed aggregation SELECT AVG(x) FROM s GROUP BY k WINDOW TUMBLING(ts, 1 SEC) lowers and pipelines into:
Pipeline A: [Source(s) → AggregationBuild]
Pipeline B: [AggregationProbe → Sink]
Pipeline A executes whenever a source-emitted WorkTask lands. Pipeline B executes when a window fires (driven by watermarks from pipeline A). The hash map is owned by the aggregation handler; pipeline A inserts, pipeline B walks and emits.

11.6 Summary
The pipelining phase converts a physical plan into a DAG of pipelines, each pipeline being a chain of operators the JIT can fuse into a single function. Pipeline breaks happen at sinks and at the build half of stateful operator pairs. Within a pipeline, operators communicate through the Record interface, which the JIT lowers to direct memory accesses. Across pipelines, operators communicate through shared operator handlers, scheduled as independent WorkTasks by the runtime. The output of pipelining plus JIT is a CompiledQueryPlan carrying both the executable stages and the fully-specified source/sink descriptors needed by the worker.
