title: 12  JIT Code Generation with Nautilus and MLIR
text:
12.1 12.1 The problem: why interpret is too slow
If you remember one thing about NebulaStream, remember this: it JIT-compiles every query. There is no interpreter on the hot path in production mode; there is no operator-by-operator dispatch; there is no virtual function call between operators. The query becomes native machine code, and the data flows through that code as fast as the hardware can move it.
The framework that makes this happen is called Nautilus. It lives in nes-nautilus/. This chapter is about how it works.
The mechanism is unusual enough that we will spend a few pages on the idea before opening any code. Tracing JITs are common in managed-runtime worlds (PyPy, V8) but rare in C++ database engines. NebulaStream’s choice to use one is the most consequential architectural decision in the system, and it deserves the careful introduction.
Imagine an operator-tree interpreter for the simple query SELECT value FROM demo WHERE value > 0. The interpreter, for each input tuple, walks:
Each next() is a virtual function call. Between calls, the interpreter has to box and unbox values, dispatch on their types, check for nulls. The actual work — comparing value to 0 and forwarding it — is a fraction of the cost. The rest is interpretation overhead.
For OLTP this overhead is fine — a transaction touches a handful of tuples and the overhead is negligible per query. For analytical workloads over millions of tuples, the overhead is the bottleneck. Hyper (Neumann 2011) established that compiling each query into a native function eliminates the overhead and yields 10-100x speedups on analytical workloads. Every modern analytical engine has followed suit: Spark Catalyst, Flink Janino, ClickHouse, DuckDB, Arrow Acero, Materialize all compile.
Stream engines need this for the same reason. A 1 MHz stream of sensor readings is, over a day, 86 billion tuples. Saving 100 ns per tuple in interpretation overhead saves 2.4 hours of CPU time.

title: 12  JIT Code Generation with Nautilus and MLIR
section: 12.2 12.2 Two approaches: AST emission vs. tracing
text:
12.2 12.2 Two approaches: AST emission vs. tracing
Once you have decided to compile, you have two broad choices:
AST emission. Each operator emits its own piece of IR (LLVM, or some intermediate language) at compile time. The compiler strings the operator-emitted pieces together. Each operator is, in effect, a code generator that knows how to emit itself. This is how Hyper, Umbra, and most database codegen frameworks work.
Tracing. Each operator is a normal C++ class whose execute method is written as if to be interpreted. The framework runs the operator once with special “tracing values” — values that record every operation performed on them. The recorded operations form an IR. The IR is compiled to native code.
The two approaches differ in where the smarts live. AST emission puts the smarts in the operator: each operator knows how to emit its own code. Tracing puts the smarts in the framework: operators are just C++ that the framework records.
Tracing has a real ergonomic advantage. To add a new operator in an AST-emission system, you write code that emits IR — a significantly different mental model from writing code that does the operation directly. To add a new operator in a tracing system, you write code that does the operation, using the framework’s typed values. The tracing system records what you did and turns it into IR for you.
NebulaStream’s Nautilus framework uses tracing. This is, to my knowledge, the only production-class C++ database engine that uses tracing-based codegen. PyPy uses tracing; V8 uses tracing; but neither is a database engine.

title: 12  JIT Code Generation with Nautilus and MLIR
text:
12.4 12.4 Trace-time vs. runtime constants
A subtlety the abbreviation glossary in docs/frequently_used_abbreviations.md flags: there are trace-time constants and runtime values. A trace-time constant is a value known when the trace runs — for example, the threshold in a selection predicate is a constant set at query compile time. A runtime value is a value known only when the compiled code runs — for example, the field of an incoming tuple.
Nautilus distinguishes the two. A trace-time constant is folded into the generated code; a runtime value becomes a load. The author of an operator does not have to think about which is which most of the time, because the type system handles it: nautilus::val<T> is runtime; a plain T (or a nautilus::val<T> constructed from a trace-time constant) is constant-folded.
This is what allows a Selection to be expressed as if (v > threshold) even though threshold differs per query: the framework specialises the generated code for the specific threshold.

section: 12.7 12.7 What goes wrong, and how the engine is built to handle it
text:
12.7 12.7 What goes wrong, and how the engine is built to handle it
Code generation is the part of the engine where mistakes are hardest to debug. A bug in a Selection is a wrong answer. A bug in the codegen for a Selection is a wrong answer that depends on the phase of the moon and the size of the alignment of an unrelated struct.
NebulaStream defends against this in a few ways.
INTERPRETER mode. Flipping execution_mode=INTERPRETER runs the same trace in the interpreter. If the answer differs from the COMPILER answer, the bug is in the lowering, not in the operator logic. We use this in essentially every reading exercise in this book.
Systests run in both modes. The CI matrix includes runs with and without compilation. A divergence between the two is caught automatically.
Trace dumps. Setting mlir.dumpIR on the engine options prints the MLIR for each compiled pipeline. For a one-operator pipeline, the IR is a screenful; the human can usually spot something obviously wrong.
The Nautilus team owns the framework. This is more sociotechnical than technical, but it matters. Bugs in Nautilus are reported to a small dedicated team that knows the lowering pipeline; bugs in operators go to the operator team. The framework boundary is also a debugging boundary.






TipReal-system reference: how Hyper does this



Hyper (Neumann 2011), the academic predecessor of Tableau’s in-memory engine, was the first system to demonstrate the value of per-query compilation. Hyper’s approach is AST emission: each operator emits LLVM IR directly through a builder API.
The operator code in Hyper looks very different from the operator code in NebulaStream. Hyper’s selection operator emits IR; NebulaStream’s selection operator does the actual operation on nautilus::val<T>. For a developer, NebulaStream’s tracing approach is much closer to writing normal code. For a runtime, the resulting native code is comparable.
The cost of tracing — and a real cost — is that the operator must be expressible in the tracing language. Operations that cannot be traced (e.g., a UDF written as a black-box function pointer) require an “extern call” mechanism that is more awkward than Hyper’s “just call the function” model.

title: 12  JIT Code Generation with Nautilus and MLIR
text:
12.8 Summary
NebulaStream’s Nautilus framework is a tracing JIT: operators are written as normal C++ that uses nautilus::val<T> for runtime values, and the framework records the operations into a trace, lowers through MLIR to LLVM IR, and JIT-compiles to native code. The runtime data structures (HashMap, PagedVector, Record) are designed for the JIT’s inlining requirements. The ExecutionMode::INTERPRETER flag runs the trace as an interpreter, which is much slower but invaluable for debugging. The choice of tracing over AST emission is unusual for a C++ database engine and is the most consequential architectural decision in NebulaStream.

title: 13  Plugin Registries and Extensibility
text:
13.1 13.1 The problem static plugins solve
The vision statement in Chapter 1 listed extensibility as one of NebulaStream’s three pillars. This chapter is about how that pillar is built — specifically, how a plugin (a new source, sink, formatter, operator, or rewrite rule) gets compiled into the engine and made discoverable at runtime, all while staying compatible with C++’s static linking model.
The mechanism is a static plugin registry, generated by CMake at build time. It is one of the more interesting pieces of build-system engineering in NebulaStream and well worth understanding before you add your first plugin.
Plugins exist to keep the engine modular. A core team can ship the engine; third parties can ship sources, sinks, and rewrite rules without touching the core code. The engine discovers plugins at runtime via a registry; user code in the engine looks up “TCP” in the source registry and gets back a factory function for constructing TCP sources.
The implementation challenge is that C++ is a static-linking language. Unlike Java or Python, where adding a class to the classpath at runtime is a normal thing, C++ wants every symbol resolved at link time. There are dynamic loading mechanisms (dlopen, LoadLibrary) but they are awkward for production deployments and disastrous for embedded targets.
NebulaStream’s solution: every plugin is statically linked, and self-registers into a global registry at startup. This is the classic “register a class with itself” pattern. The trick is doing it without falling into the Static Initialisation Order Fiasco (SIOF) — the well-known C++ pitfall where the order of static initialisations across translation units is undefined.
The full solution is documented in docs/design/20240701_static_plugin_registry.md. The mechanism has five stated goals (G1–G5):
The fix for G5 is what makes the design interesting.

title: 13  Plugin Registries and Extensibility
text:
G1: Plugins must be statically linkable and self-register.
G2: Internal vs. external plugins must be cleanly separated.
G3: The mechanism must work for many extension types (sources, sinks, operators, types, functions, rewrite rules).
G4: Registration must be guaranteed (no “I forgot to declare this static instance” failures).
G5: Must not depend on initialisation order.

if (NES_ENABLES_TESTS)
    activate_optional_plugin("Sinks/ChecksumSink" ON)
endif()
activate_optional_plugin turns on an optional plugin in the build. There is a corresponding add_plugin for built-in plugins that ship in the engine without an opt-in toggle.
What the macros actually do, behind the scenes, is generate a Registrar class — a single C++ file that contains, for each active plugin, the registration call. The generation is in generate_plugin_registrar:
# cmake/PluginRegistrationUtil.cmake (excerpt)
function(generate_plugin_registrar current_dir current_binary_dir
                                   plugin_registry plugin_registry_component)
    set(registrar_header_template_path
        ${current_dir}/registry/templates/${plugin_registry}GeneratedRegistrar.inc.in)
    file(READ ${registrar_header_template_path} registrar_header_file_data)

    foreach (reg_func IN LISTS plugin_registry_plugin_names_final)
        list(APPEND REGISTER_FUNCTION_DECLARATIONS
             "${plugin_registry}RegistryReturnType Register${reg_func}${plugin_registry}(${plugin_registry}RegistryArguments)")
        list(APPEND REGISTER_ALL_FUNCTION_CALLS
             "registry.addEntry(\"${reg_func}\", Register${reg_func}${plugin_registry})")
    endforeach ()

    configure_file(${temp_registrar_header_template_file}
                   ${registrar_header_generated_path} @ONLY)
endfunction()
The template file (<Type>GeneratedRegistrar.inc.in) declares forward declarations for every plugin’s Register* function and a single registerAll method that calls each. The plugin author provides the Register* function in their plugin code; CMake generates the file that calls them all.

title: 13  Plugin Registries and Extensibility
text:
13.3 13.3 The eager-init escape from SIOF
The Static Initialisation Order Fiasco arises when one global constructor uses another that has not yet been constructed. Self-registration through static MyPlugin instance{} traditionally suffers from this: which plugin’s constructor runs first? Which finds the registry already initialised?
NebulaStream sidesteps this with explicit initialisation:

The registry is not a global. It is created on-demand when first accessed (Meyers’ singleton pattern), so its lifetime begins at first use.
Plugin registration is not a static constructor. It is a function call inside registerAll, which is invoked explicitly from main() (or an equivalent fixed initialisation point in the worker startup).

The result is that registration order is well-defined: it is the order of registerAll’s sequential calls. The compiler is not asked to make any guarantee about cross-translation-unit ordering.
This is, in retrospect, the obvious solution. Most “self-registering plugin” patterns in C++ get this wrong; NebulaStream’s design is one of the cleaner implementations I have seen.

13.5 13.5 Adding a new source: a worked example
Adding a new source plugin is the canonical “hello world” of NebulaStream extensibility. The full walkthrough is in docs/guide/extensibility.md and docs/guide/how_to_add_a_source.md. The shape:

Create a new directory under nes-plugins/Sources/MySource/ (alongside the existing nes-plugins/Sources/TCPSource/) with a CMakeLists.txt and the plugin’s source files.
The CMakeLists.txt calls add_plugin_as_library with the plugin name and the registry it belongs to.
The plugin’s source provides a Register* function that the generated Registrar will call. The function body adds the factory function to the registry.
Activate the plugin in nes-plugins/CMakeLists.txt with activate_optional_plugin("Sources/MySource" ON).
Rebuild. The CMake regeneration picks up the new entry, the Registrar is regenerated, the worker’s startup code calls the plugin’s Register*, and “MySource” is now a valid TYPE in CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE statements.

That is the entire user-facing surface: write a class, write a register function, add a CMake line, rebuild. No symbol-table contortions, no dynamic loading, no dlopen.






TipReal-system reference: how Telegraf and PostgreSQL handle this



Telegraf’s plugin system is a register-by-function-pointer pattern in Go, which has language-level support for init() functions that the runtime calls at startup. The mechanism is much simpler than NebulaStream’s CMake template machinery — but of course it requires a runtime. C++ does not have one.
PostgreSQL’s plugin system is dynamic: shared libraries (postgresql-contrib packages) are loaded with LOAD 'mymodule' at runtime, with each module’s _PG_init() doing registration. This is more flexible (you can add modules without rebuilding the server) but more dangerous (ABI compatibility is the user’s problem) and not viable for embedded deployments.
NebulaStream’s static-linked, CMake-generated registrar is the right answer for an engine targeting edge deployments where runtime dynamic loading is awkward and a rebuild is the expected mode of customisation.

title: 13  Plugin Registries and Extensibility
text:
13.6 Summary
NebulaStream’s plugin system is a static plugin registry generated at CMake-time. The framework supports sources, sinks, input/output formatters, and lowering rules through a single uniform mechanism: a string-keyed factory registry, populated by an explicitly-called registerAll function whose body is generated by CMake from a template. The design avoids the Static Initialisation Order Fiasco by replacing constructor-time self-registration with explicit initialisation. Adding a new plugin is a directory, a CMake line, and a Register* function — no dynamic loading, no manual registry edits.

title: 14  Task-Based Execution Model
text:
14.1 14.1 The lifetime of a query: three states
A query plan is a static description of what to compute. A running query is the dynamic process of computing it. The bridge between the two is the execution model: how operators get scheduled, how state is held while operators run, how the lifecycle of a query is managed.
NebulaStream’s execution model is task-based. Every unit of work — processing a TupleBuffer, starting a pipeline, stopping a source, firing a window — is a typed Task. Worker threads consume tasks from the queue (Chapter 15), execute them, and emit follow-up tasks. There is no separate control plane; lifecycle and data flow share the same queue.
This chapter walks through the data structures: ExecutableQueryPlan, RunningQueryPlan, RunningSource, the Task variant. We have already met the queue in Chapter 15; now we look at what it schedules.
A query passes through three states inside the engine:
Compiled. A CompiledQueryPlan is the artefact produced by the compile pipeline (Chapter 11). It is a passive description: function pointers, source descriptors, sink descriptors. Nothing runs yet.
Executable. When the engine accepts a CompiledQueryPlan, it constructs an ExecutableQueryPlan from it. The executable wraps the compiled stages with runtime context: per-pipeline operator handlers, callbacks for completion, identifiers. Still passive, but ready to be started.
Running. When the user (or the engine’s auto-start logic) asks the engine to start the query, the executable becomes a RunningQueryPlan plus per-pipeline RunningQueryPlanNodes plus per-source RunningSources. The sources begin emitting WorkTasks. The query is alive.
These states are not just naming conventions. They correspond to distinct types in nes-query-engine/:
The transitions are explicit StartQueryTask and StopQueryTask operations, scheduled through the same task queue as data work.

text:
14.4 14.4 RunningSource: a source instance lifecycle
The runtime counterpart of a Source (Chapter 8) is a RunningSource, in nes-query-engine/RunningSource.hpp. The RunningSource wraps a SourceHandle (the constructed source instance) and manages its lifecycle:

Start. A worker thread accepts a StartPipelineTask for the source’s source-pipeline; the running source begins reading from its underlying source (fillTupleBuffer) and emitting WorkTasks into the admission queue.
Stop. A StopSourceTask triggers a graceful shutdown. The source stops reading; in-flight buffers continue to flow.
Fail. A FailSourceTask arrives if the source raises an exception (e.g., the file disappears, the TCP connection resets). The source is torn down; the query catalog is notified.

RunningSource has its own state machine. Sources can be STARTING, RUNNING, STOPPING, STOPPED. The transitions are serialised through the same task queue, ensuring that a source cannot, for example, attempt to emit a WorkTask while it is mid-shutdown.

14.6 14.6 Worker threads, work emitters, lifetime controllers
The worker side of the engine has two interfaces, in nes-query-engine/Interfaces.hpp:

WorkEmitter — the abstract interface a worker uses to emit a follow-up task. The implementation is the engine’s internal queue; the interface keeps the worker decoupled from the queue type. (This is the same interface that makes it easy to mock the queue for tests.)
QueryLifetimeController — the abstract interface for lifecycle changes (start, stop, fail). Concrete implementations push tasks into the queue.

These interfaces give the worker a small, stable contract. The worker does not know that it is using two folly queues; it knows that there is something it can put work into and something it can ask about query lifetime.

title: 14  Task-Based Execution Model
section: 14.7 14.6 Putting it together: a tuple’s journey
text:
14.7 14.6 Putting it together: a tuple’s journey
To pull all these threads together, here is the journey of a single tuple through the running engine, from source to sink:

A RunningSource for source demo calls Source::fillTupleBuffer and gets back an 8 KiB buffer with, say, 1024 tuples.
The running source wraps the buffer in a WorkTask and writes it to the admission queue via WorkEmitter::emit.
A worker thread dequeues the WorkTask. It is for pipeline 1 (the source pipeline).
The worker locks the weak_ptr in the task to the RunningQueryPlanNode for pipeline 1. Increments pendingTasks.
The worker invokes the compiled function pointer for pipeline 1 on the buffer. The function loops over the 1024 tuples, processes each (in our demo: identity projection), and writes them to the sink’s output formatter.
As tuples are processed, the compiled code emits one or more follow-up WorkTasks if the pipeline has downstream consumers beyond the sink. (For our demo, there are no downstreams; the sink is the end.)
The function returns. The worker decrements pendingTasks.
If the buffer originated as a source emission, the source’s completion callback runs.

Steps 1–8 typically execute in microseconds for a small buffer. The queue, the weak_ptr lock, and the function call together add on the order of 100 ns of overhead per buffer; the rest is operator work.
In a distributed deployment (Chapter 19), one further step is inserted at any pipeline boundary that crosses a worker: a NetworkSink serialises the buffer onto a Rust-side channel, and a NetworkSource deserialises it on the other side. From the worker’s point of view the network sink/source pair looks identical to any other sink/source pair; the data plane between workers is the only piece that knows it is crossing a network.

title: 14  Task-Based Execution Model
text:
14.8 Summary
The execution model is task-based and unified: data work and lifecycle work share a single typed Task variant, dispatched through std::visit. Pipelines are runtime objects (RunningQueryPlanNode) with reference counts that gate graceful shutdown. Sources are wrapped in RunningSource instances with their own state machines. Worker threads use small abstract interfaces (WorkEmitter, QueryLifetimeController) that decouple them from the queue and lifecycle implementation. The combination gives the engine a uniform model: every action is a task; every worker is a task processor.

title: 15  The Two-Queue Scheduler and Deadlock Avoidance
text:
15.1 15.1 The problem: a bounded queue and two ways to deadlock
A stream processing engine is, at its heart, a machine for moving tuples between stateful operators. The scheduler decides which operator runs next and on which worker thread. Get it wrong and the engine either starves under load, livelocks under pressure, or — most embarrassingly — deadlocks itself into a frozen process that has to be killed and restarted.
In this chapter we open up NebulaStream’s scheduler. The structure we will examine is, in code, fewer than two hundred lines. The reasons it exists, the bugs that pushed it to its current shape, and the trade-offs it embodies — those take the rest of the chapter.
We will not start with the solution. We will start with the bug.
Most production stream engines distribute work across a pool of worker threads using a shared task queue. Worker threads dequeue tasks, do some work, and emit follow-up tasks back to the queue. Sources also emit tasks: when a CSV file source reads a fresh batch of bytes and parses it into a TupleBuffer, it emits a task instructing some downstream pipeline to consume that buffer.
In an idealised version of this design, the queue is unbounded. A task is always accepted, the producer never has to wait, and you only need to decide on dequeue order. In practice, an unbounded queue is a way to crash later. Memory is finite; if a fast source can permanently out-produce the workers, the queue grows without bound and the process exhausts its address space. The fix, almost reflexively, is to make the queue bounded.
Then you have a different problem.
A bounded queue, by definition, can be full. If a producer tries to write to a full queue, you have three choices: drop the task, return an error, or block the producer until space is available. Stream engines almost always choose to block — dropping or erroring would break the engine’s processing guarantees. Blocking the producer is called backpressure and it is the right answer. It is also the answer that introduces deadlocks.
There are two distinct ways the engine can deadlock against its own bounded queue. NebulaStream’s design document for the query engine calls them P1 and P2 (NebulaStream contributors 2024). We will use the same labels.
P1 — worker-emission deadlock. A worker thread holding a task attempts to emit a follow-up task. The queue is full. The thread blocks waiting for capacity. But capacity will only become available when some other worker thread dequeues a task, finishes it, and emits its own follow-up. If every worker is in the same emit-and-block state, no worker dequeues. The system deadlocks.
This is not a hypothetical scenario. It is what happens during a hash join probe, where each input tuple may produce many output tuples; or during a window trigger, where firing a window emits a fan-out of downstream work. In both cases, a single dequeued task can produce many emitted tasks, and the queue can fill from the inside out.
P2 — source-flooding deadlock. Sources are not workers. A source thread does not dequeue tasks; it only emits them. If the source is faster than the workers — say, a high-rate sensor or a Kafka topic being replayed at full speed — the source can fill the queue with unprocessed tuples faster than the workers drain it. Once the queue is full, the source blocks; once the source blocks, no new work enters; the workers drain the queue and idle. Then the source unblocks and the cycle resumes. This is not a deadlock in the strict sense (the system makes progress eventually) but it has two ugly consequences. First, the workers cycle between full saturation and complete idleness. The throughput of the system is dictated by the queue size and not by the hardware. Second — more dangerously — if the worker emits a follow-up task while the queue is saturated by source-emitted tasks, the worker also blocks. Now we are back in P1.
The two problems sound similar but they have different fixes. We will solve them separately.

NoteExample 15.1: P1 in a hash join probe



Consider a hash join with two input streams R and S. The build side R has been hashed into an in-memory hash table. A WorkTask arrives for S: process this 8 KiB batch of S tuples. The probe finds matches for, on average, 1.7 tuples per input tuple, so the batch produces a follow-up batch about 1.7× as large.
The worker dequeues the S-side WorkTask, performs the probe, and now needs to emit a follow-up WorkTask for the next operator downstream. If every worker thread is in this state — having just dequeued an S task and trying to emit a probe-result task — and the queue is full, no worker can emit and no worker can dequeue. That is P1.

15.5 15.5 The semaphore invariant
The invariant printed in the comment on line 40 is doing the heavy lifting:

INVARIANT: internal.size() + admission.size() >= tasksAvailable

The sum of the two queue sizes is at least equal to the semaphore counter. The semaphore counter is the engine’s notion of “how many tasks are available right now.” That count must never exceed the real number of tasks, or a worker thread will be told that work exists when in fact it does not, and the worker will spin or fail.
The invariant is upheld by carefully ordering the operations on each write path. Both addAdmissionTaskBlocking and addInternalTaskNonBlocking release the semaphore only after the task has actually been enqueued. On the dequeue side, the worker first acquires the semaphore (blocking if the count is zero) and only then attempts to read the task. The acquire is the worker’s promise that a task exists. The semaphore is the only synchronisation between writer and reader visible to the queue’s API.
This is the kind of invariant that, on paper, is a single line. In a production system, it is tested against thousands of randomised producer/consumer interleavings. NebulaStream’s tests/TaskQueueTest.cpp exercises this directly with a multi-producer, multi-consumer fuzzer that reasons about the order of writes vs. reads to expose any window in which the invariant could be violated.

section: 15.6 15.6 The Task variant: not all tasks are workunits
text:
15.6 15.6 The Task variant: not all tasks are workunits
We have been speaking as if “task” meant only “process this batch of tuples.” It does not. The task type is a std::variant of eight distinct task kinds, defined in nes-query-engine/Task.hpp:195-203:
using Task = std::variant<
    WorkTask,
    StopQueryTask,
    StartQueryTask,
    FailSourceTask,
    StopSourceTask,
    PendingPipelineStopTask,
    StopPipelineTask,
    StartPipelineTask>;
WorkTask is the one we have been discussing: process tuples in a specific buffer through a specific pipeline node. The other seven control the lifecycle of queries, sources and pipelines. They flow through the same queue infrastructure as data because the engine has chosen to model “stop this pipeline” and “process this tuple” as the same kind of event: a thing the worker thread does next.
The choice is unusual. Many engines model lifecycle changes as out-of-band signals — a separate control plane, sometimes a separate thread. NebulaStream multiplexes them onto the worker queue. The benefit is that lifecycle changes are naturally serialised against data: a StopQueryTask cannot accidentally race with the data it is trying to stop, because it is processed by a worker between two data tasks. The cost is that lifecycle work blocks behind data work, and the engine has to be careful to ensure lifecycle work is not starved.






NoteExample 15.3: a query stop is just another task



A user submits STOP QUERY 42. The frontend translates this into a StopQueryTask and writes it to the admission queue. The admission queue is currently full of WorkTasks for query 42. The StopQueryTask waits.
A worker thread picks up the next admitted task — say, a WorkTask for query 42. It processes the tuples. Now the worker dequeues again, finds the StopQueryTask, and runs it: the query catalog is consulted, the pipelines are torn down, the sources are signalled to stop.
The query stop is naturally serialised behind the work that was already in flight. There is no race between “process tuple 9 in query 42” and “stop query 42” because they happen on the same worker thread, in queue order.


The most interesting member of the variant — the one that motivates the rest of this chapter — is PendingPipelineStopTask.

text:
15.9 15.9 Putting it together: the worker loop
We have now seen all the pieces. Let us assemble them into a single mental model of the worker loop.






Figure 15.1: The worker thread loop. The wait at top is bounded by StopTokenCheckInterval (100 ms) so cancellation has bounded latency. Every code path eventually returns to the wait, except the Worker exits exit on shutdown.



Each loop iteration does at most one of: (a) acquire and process a single task, (b) time out and check for shutdown. There is no spinning, no polling, no busy work between tasks. The only place a worker thread waits is on tasksAvailable.try_acquire_for, and that wait is bounded by StopTokenCheckInterval.
Source threads and external producers run a parallel loop with a different shape: they emit tasks via addAdmissionTaskBlocking and their throughput is bounded by the admission queue’s capacity.
The two loops meet at one point: the semaphore. The semaphore is the only piece of synchronisation that workers and producers share. The queues themselves are lock-free (folly’s MPMC and UMPMC are both implemented atop atomics, with no mutexes on the hot paths). The combination — lock-free data structures synchronised by a counting semaphore that doubles as a cancellation point — is what gives the scheduler its blend of low overhead and clean shutdown semantics.






TipReal-system reference: Materialize and timely dataflow



Materialize is built on differential dataflow (McSherry et al. 2013), which uses a fundamentally different scheduling model: a frontier of timestamps that operators advance cooperatively, with no central queue. Each worker thread owns a slice of the operator graph and runs operators round-robin against their pending work.
Timely dataflow’s strength is fine-grained progress reasoning; NebulaStream’s strength (with its central two-queue scheduler) is operational simplicity. The two designs sit on opposite ends of the “how distributed should the scheduler itself be” spectrum.

title: 15  The Two-Queue Scheduler and Deadlock Avoidance
section: 15.10 15.10 What this design does not do
text:
15.10 15.10 What this design does not do
It is worth being explicit about what the two-queue scheduler does not attempt.
It does not prioritise tasks. The design document is explicit on this point (NebulaStream contributors 2024, §Scope): “It does not perform any prioritization of tasks in terms of latency or throughput, but prevents deadlocks.” A latency-sensitive query and a throughput- oriented query share the same queue and are processed in arrival order. If a future version of the engine wants per-query scheduling policies, the queue infrastructure will need to be replaced or augmented; the current design is silent on the question.
It does not implement work stealing in the strict sense. Work stealing, as in Cilk or Tokio’s multi-threaded executor, gives each worker a private deque and lets idle workers steal from busy ones’ deques. NebulaStream has a single shared queue (well, two), and workers race to dequeue from it. The behaviour is similar — idle workers always pick up available work — but the mechanism is classical shared-queue work distribution, not work stealing.
It does not model per-pipeline backpressure. As we saw in the Flink sidebar, some engines push backpressure through the operator graph itself. NebulaStream’s backpressure is global: when the admission queue is full, all sources block, regardless of which pipeline is the bottleneck. A slow downstream operator backpressures fast upstream sources, but only because the workers are busy and cannot drain fast enough — there is no targeted signal to throttle a specific source. This is fine for the engine’s current scale; if NebulaStream grows to thousands of concurrent queries with very heterogeneous resource needs, it will likely need a more discriminating mechanism.
It is per-worker, not cross-worker. Each NebulaStream worker has its own pair of queues and its own pool of worker threads. In a distributed deployment (Chapter 19), task scheduling is local to each worker; the network channels between workers are the only inter-worker coordination, and they speak in TupleBuffers, not in Tasks. Backpressure across workers travels through the network channels (Chapter 19’s backpressure{Upper,Lower}Threshold settings) rather than through the task queue. This is one of the cleaner consequences of the decomposition strategy: a per-worker scheduler has no global state to share, which is exactly what makes adding more workers a question of “spin one up” rather than “reconfigure the scheduler.”
These are deliberate non-goals. The two-queue design is, by C++ standards of fanciness, almost embarrassingly modest. Two folly queues. One semaphore. One stop token. About two hundred lines of code, including tests. The lesson is not that the scheduler is small because the problem is small. The lesson is that the scheduler is small because the problems it does not solve are handled elsewhere — the buffer manager handles memory pressure, the optimiser handles operator placement, the source registry handles source-specific backpressure. The scheduler does one thing: it gets work to workers without deadlocking.

title: 15  The Two-Queue Scheduler and Deadlock Avoidance
text:
15.11 Summary
A bounded shared task queue is the natural starting point for a scheduler in a stream processing engine, but it leaves you with two deadlock surfaces: worker-emission deadlock (P1) and source-flooding deadlock (P2).
NebulaStream solves them with a structural separation: two queues, each with different blocking semantics. The internal queue is unbounded and never blocks a worker on emit, eliminating P1. The admission queue is bounded and blocks producers, providing the backpressure that keeps the engine from running out of memory while preventing source floods from starving worker emissions, eliminating P2. The two queues are unified for the worker via a std::counting_semaphore whose count is the engine’s authoritative notion of “work available.”
Cancellation is layered on top of both blocking calls via a 100 ms poll on a std::stop_token, which gives shutdown a bounded latency without measurable steady-state cost.
A subtle third failure mode — a self-emitting PendingPipelineStopTask that monopolises the internal queue — is handled by a small backoff mechanism that routes the task through a DelayedTaskSubmitter after two failed attempts, ensuring source-emitted work in the admission queue gets a chance to advance.
The design is deliberately minimal. Per-task prioritisation, per-pipeline backpressure, and work stealing are all deferred to other parts of the engine or to future work. What is left is small, fast, and — most important — provably free of the two deadlock surfaces that motivated its existence.

16.1 16.1 The state architecture: handlers, hash maps, and PagedVectors
Stateless operators have it easy. A Selection, a Map, a Projection — each takes a record, transforms it, forwards it. Nothing remembered, nothing to clean up, nothing that can grow unbounded.
Stateful operators are where streaming gets interesting. A hash join build accumulates one side of the join. A windowed aggregation accumulates partial sums per group per window. A session window operator accumulates per-session bookkeeping until the session times out. State is the engine’s memory of what has happened, and it has to be kept correct, kept bounded, and kept usable across worker threads.
This chapter walks through how NebulaStream manages stateful operator state. The data structures are the runtime ones we met in Chapter 12 (HashMap, PagedVector); the lifecycle is intricate enough to warrant its own chapter.
Every stateful operator in NebulaStream owns its state through an operator handler. The handler is a runtime object — distinct from the operator class itself — that holds the per-query state and exposes it to both the build and probe halves of the operator pair.
Handlers are registered at query-startup time, identified by an OperatorHandlerId, and torn down when the pipeline that owns them is destroyed. The OperatorHandlerId is the join’s “shared key” — the build operator references it to know where to insert; the probe operator references the same one to know where to look up.
The state itself almost always combines two structures:
Both come from nes-nautilus/; both are designed for the JIT to inline.

A HashMap keyed on the join key (or the grouping key). The hash map holds entries, each a fixed-size header plus a pointer to a value chain.
A PagedVector of values for chained collisions or unbounded per-key history.

text:
16.3 16.3 Aggregation state
A windowed aggregation’s state is also a hash map, but the values are partial aggregates, not records:

For SUM(x): value is (running_sum, count).
For AVG(x): value is (running_sum, count), with the average computed at probe time.
For MIN(x): value is (running_min).
For COUNT(*): value is (count).

These are small, fixed-size, and combinable. The build side combines incoming tuples into partial aggregates; the probe side, when a window fires, walks the hash map and emits one record per key with the final aggregate value.
For sliding windows where multiple windows can be live simultaneously, the state grows linearly in the number of active windows. The engine partitions state by window: each (window, key) pair gets its own hash-map entry. When a window fires and all sliding windows that include the same data have either fired or been GC’d, the state for that window is freed.

title: 16  Stateful Operators and State Management
text:
16.5 16.5 Concurrent state, safely
State is shared between worker threads. Multiple workers can simultaneously be inserting into the same build’s hash map, or probing the same join’s state, or accumulating into the same window’s partial aggregates.
NebulaStream handles concurrency in three layers.
Lock-free at the hash-map level. The hash map’s insertion uses atomic CAS for slot acquisition. Two workers inserting different keys do not contend; two workers inserting the same key contend briefly on the value-chain head pointer.
Per-window watermark coordination. Two watermark processors live on each WindowBasedOperatorHandler: one tracks the build side, one tracks the probe side. The watermarks are advanced atomically; a window’s transition from “open” to “ready to fire” is a single atomic check.
Coarse-grained for less-contended state. State that is not on the hot path (the slice store metadata, the per-handler GC list) is protected by a folly::Synchronized wrapper, which is essentially a mutex with a more ergonomic API.
The engine chooses lock-freedom on the hot paths and locks elsewhere — the standard concurrent-data-structures trade-off.
crumbs: 16  Stateful Operators and State Management

title: 16  Stateful Operators and State Management
text:
16.6 16.6 Garbage collection
State has to be released. The engine releases it conservatively via the slice-and-watermark machinery from Chapter 7:

A slice is “complete” when all upstream watermarks have passed the slice’s end time.
A complete slice is “fired” — its windows trigger and emit results.
After firing, the slice is “garbage” — eligible for release.
The handler’s garbageCollectSlicesAndWindows walks the garbage list and frees the underlying buffers.

The release is to the buffer pool, not to the OS. Buffers go back into the pool’s queue and are immediately available for reuse by fresh state.
Late-arriving data that targets a freed slice is dropped, not re-incorporated. This matches the engine’s overall stance: when in doubt, prefer correctness over leniency. Flink’s “late side output” mechanism would be a future addition.
A note worth making before this chapter ends: NebulaStream’s execution-state — the hash maps and PagedVectors we have been discussing — is in-memory only. There is no checkpointing path yet that would let a worker crash and resume from a snapshot. What does exist is a small piece of client-side query metadata persistence in nes-frontend/apps/cli/QueryStateBackend.hpp that records query IDs and timestamps under ~/.local/state/nebucli/. That is REPL/CLI bookkeeping, not execution-state recovery. The two are easy to confuse; Chapter 22 spells out the difference.

title: 16  Stateful Operators and State Management
text:
16.7 Summary
Stateful operators in NebulaStream own their state through operator handlers, which are runtime objects identified by an OperatorHandlerId and shared between the build and probe halves of the operator. The state is almost always a HashMap keyed on the operator’s grouping/join key, possibly with a PagedVector for collision chains or per-key history. Both data structures are paged across TupleBuffers from the buffer pool, allowing release back to the pool when a slice’s lifetime ends. Concurrency is handled by lock-free CAS on the hot path and folly::Synchronized locks elsewhere. State is garbage-collected slice-by-slice as watermarks advance; late-arriving data targeting freed slices is silently dropped.

title: 17  Error Handling, Logging, and Observability
text:
17.1 17.1 Bugs vs. errors
A streaming engine cannot fail silently. A query that produces wrong answers is worse than a query that crashes. NebulaStream treats error handling as a first-class concern: there is a written design document for it (docs/design/20240711_error_handling.md), a centralised exception list, two assertion macros for invariants, and a discipline of distinguishing recoverable errors from bugs.
This chapter walks through the discipline.
The first useful distinction is also the bluntest: some failures are bugs (the code is wrong) and some are errors (the world is wrong). They warrant different handling.
A bug is a violation of an invariant the code maintains. The worker dequeued a task whose pipeline weak_ptr was supposed to be non-null but is null. The hash map’s getNumberOfTuples returned a value larger than its capacity. These are facts about the code’s internal consistency that, if violated, mean the code has a defect the user cannot work around. The right response is to fail loudly and crash; continuing is dangerous.
An error is an external condition the code anticipated. The file source was given a path that does not exist. A field in the input failed to parse as UINT64. The TCP source’s connection dropped mid-stream. These are facts about the world the engine has no control over. The right response is to handle them — either recover, or report a clean error to the user.
NebulaStream uses different mechanisms for the two:
We will see each.

Bugs: INVARIANT and PRECONDITION macros. Crash on violation.
Errors: typed exceptions. Throw on unrecoverable failure; return std::expected<T, Exception> or std::optional<T> for expected-but-unsuccessful outcomes.

17.2 17.2 The exception list: one file, eighty types
NebulaStream has a single file that defines every exception type it can throw. The file is nes-common/include/ExceptionDefinitions.inc. Each entry uses an EXCEPTION macro:
// nes-common/include/ExceptionDefinitions.inc (sketch)
EXCEPTION(InvalidConfigParameter, 1000, "Invalid configuration parameter")
EXCEPTION(CannotLoadConfig, 1001, "Cannot load configuration file")
// ... ~80 more entries ...
EXCEPTION(InvalidQuerySyntax, 2000, "Invalid query syntax")
EXCEPTION(UnknownSourceType, 2017, "Unknown source type")
EXCEPTION(QueryCompilerError, 2032, "Query compiler error")
EXCEPTION(BufferAllocationFailure, 3000, "Buffer allocation failed")
EXCEPTION(QueryNotRegistered, 3001, "Query not registered")
EXCEPTION(ArithmeticalError, 3013, "Arithmetic error")
EXCEPTION(CannotConnectToCoordinator, 5000, "Cannot connect to coordinator")
EXCEPTION(InternalErrorAssert, 9000, "Internal error - assertion violated")
EXCEPTION(FunctionNotImplemented, 9001, "Function not implemented")
Three observations.
Centralisation. Every exception is in this file. New exception types are added here and only here. The CLAUDE.md guideline is explicit: “All exception types defined in a single file.” This is unusual — most C++ codebases scatter exception definitions across translation units — and it is unusually useful: you can grep one file to know everything that can go wrong.
Numeric codes by category. The four-digit codes group exceptions by error class. The verified taxonomy as of origin/main is:

Total: 70 exception types, all defined in one file. A user-visible error message includes the code; an operator seeing error 4004: Cannot open sink can distinguish “the output path is bad” from error 2300: Placement failure (“the ILP solver could not place this query”).
The 23XX block is worth calling out separately. Distributed deployments (Chapter 19) introduce four error modes — the ILP fails, a topology cycle is detected, an unknown worker is referenced, or a worker-side failure propagates to the coordinator. They live as a sub-block of 2XXX rather than their own range because, conceptually, all four are “compilation/registration” failures: they happen before or during query startup, not during steady-state execution. The 5XXX network range covers in-flight network errors.
Structured construction. The EXCEPTION macro generates a constructor that supports fmt::format-style formatting:
// (Sketch of what EXCEPTION expands to)
inline Exception InvalidConfigParameter() {
    return Exception("Invalid configuration parameter", 1000);
}
inline Exception InvalidConfigParameter(std::string msg) {
    return Exception(fmt::format("Invalid configuration parameter; {}\n", msg), 1000);
}
template <typename... Args>
inline Exception InvalidConfigParameter(fmt::format_string<Args...> fmt_msg, Args&&... args) {
    return Exception(
        fmt::format("Invalid configuration parameter; {}\n",
                    fmt::format(fmt_msg, std::forward<Args>(args)...)),
        1000);
}
throw InvalidConfigParameter("port {} is out of range", 99999) produces a message that the caller can format and the user can read.

title: 17  Error Handling, Logging, and Observability
text:
17.3 17.3 INVARIANT and PRECONDITION
For bugs, NebulaStream uses two macros, both in nes-common/include/ErrorHandling.hpp:
// nes-common/include/ErrorHandling.hpp
#define INVARIANT(condition, formatString, ...)                                \
    do {                                                                        \
        if (!(condition)) {                                                    \
            auto trace = cpptrace::generate_trace().to_string(true);           \
            NES_ERROR("Invariant violated: ({}): " formatString "\n\n{}",      \
                      #condition __VA_OPT__(, ) __VA_ARGS__, trace);           \
            if (auto logger = ::NES::Logger::getInstance())                    \
                logger->shutdown();                                            \
            std::terminate();                                                  \
        }                                                                      \
    } while (false)
INVARIANT(condition, fmt, args…) checks a condition that should be true if the engine’s logic is correct. On violation, it produces a stack trace via cpptrace, logs at ERROR level, flushes the logger, and terminates. There is no recovery path; the engine crashes.
PRECONDITION is the symmetric macro for function entry: a condition the caller is supposed to ensure. Same mechanics, same crash-on-violation behaviour.
Both macros are compiled away in Release and Benchmark builds (via #define NO_ASSERT). In Debug and RelWithDebInfo, they fire. The reasoning is conventional: production should not pay the cost of internal-consistency checks; development should pay the cost generously.






NoteExample 17.1: when INVARIANT fires



A worker thread dequeues a WorkTask and locks its weak_ptr to a RunningQueryPlanNode. The lock fails (returns nullptr). The worker logs and drops the task — that is graceful, not a bug. But suppose the worker’s own state says it should have a non-null pointer at this point: the worker just locked a weak_ptr two lines up and stored the result, and now the result is nullptr. That would be:
INVARIANT(strongRef != nullptr,
          "RunningQueryPlanNode disappeared mid-handler for query {}",
          task.queryId);
If this fires, something has destroyed the node while a worker held a strong reference to it — which the engine’s lifecycle machinery should make impossible. The crash is correct: the alternative is undefined behaviour.

17.4 17.4 Logging through spdlog
NebulaStream uses spdlog (Melman 2014--) as its logger. Configuration lives in nes-single-node-worker/src/SingleNodeWorker.cpp and the API is the standard NES_TRACE, NES_DEBUG, NES_INFO, NES_WARN, NES_ERROR macros. fmt-style formatting is the convention:

         queryId, plan.getPipelines().size());

This is the right choice for performance experiments where each remaining cycle matters; it is the wrong default for production debugging, which is why production typically uses Release rather than Benchmark.
There is also a custom GoogleEventTracePrinter that, when enabled, writes Chrome-tracing-compatible JSON for the worker. You can drag the resulting trace into chrome://tracing and visualise the worker’s activity at sub-millisecond granularity. This is one of the engine’s better debugging aids and is a standard tool we will use throughout Chapter 21 (benchmarking).

title: 17  Error Handling, Logging, and Observability
text:
17.6 17.6 Distributed failure modes
The four 23XX exception types we catalogued in Section 17.2 cover specific failure shapes the distributed layer can produce.
PlacementFailure (2300). The ILP solver returned no feasible solution. Causes: a sink was declared on a worker that has no path to the source’s worker; a query asks for more capacity than any single worker can provide; the user declared sources and sinks that the topology cannot connect. The exception travels back to the user as a registration error (the query never starts).
InvalidTopology (2301). Adding a worker would create a cycle in the DAG. Thrown by NetworkTopology::addNode (Chapter 19). This is a structural violation, not a runtime failure; the offending registration is rejected and the catalog stays consistent.
UnknownWorker (2302). The catalog was queried for a host that was never registered. Usually a programming error in the coordinator code; less commonly, a race between worker deregistration and a placement decision that referenced the worker. Either way, the engine cannot proceed safely — bare hosts have no associated WorkerConfig, so it is unsafe to guess.
DistributedFailure (2303). The catch-all for worker-side errors that propagate up. A worker reports a runtime exception to the coordinator; the coordinator wraps it in a DistributedFailure carrying the original exception’s information. The user sees the coordinator’s wrapped error; the worker’s logs carry the original.
What is not a 23XX exception: a transient network disruption. If a worker becomes unreachable mid-query, the coordinator’s DistributedQueryStatusSnapshot flips hasConnectionException and the global query status moves to Unreachable (Chapter 19). This is a state, not an exception — the engine does not throw on its own polling.
The asymmetry between “failed loud” (an exception) and “fell silent” (Unreachable) is intentional. Loud failures are problems the engine has identified; silent ones are situations the engine cannot conclude about. Forcing the second into the first would lose information.

section: 17.7 17.7 Observability: where to look when something is wrong
text:
17.7 17.7 Observability: where to look when something is wrong
Practical advice for the reader who has just hit an error in NebulaStream:

Check the log first. The error code in the message lets you grep nes-common/include/ExceptionDefinitions.inc for the declaration; the surrounding text usually points at the code path that failed.
Run with --logging.level=TRACE. TRACE is generous; it logs every task, every pipeline transition, every state change. For non-trivial bugs the answer is somewhere in the trace.
Run in INTERPRETER mode. If the bug might be in the JIT, --worker.default_query_execution.execution_mode=INTERPRETER removes the entire compilation pipeline and runs the trace directly. If the bug disappears, the bug is in code generation.
Run with sanitizers. The CLAUDE.md notes the CI builds matrix includes ASan, UBSan, and TSan. For memory-corruption-shaped bugs, a sanitizer build localises the bug almost instantly.
Use the Chrome trace. Enable GoogleEventTracePrinter and drag the JSON into chrome://tracing for a visual timeline.

The engine has invested visibly in observability. Most stream engines’ debug stories are worse.

title: 17  Error Handling, Logging, and Observability
text:
17.8 Summary
NebulaStream distinguishes bugs (handled by INVARIANT/ PRECONDITION macros that crash on violation) from recoverable errors (handled by typed exceptions or std::expected). The exception list is centralised in a single .inc file with ~80 typed exceptions organised into numeric ranges by category. Logging is through spdlog with build-type-aware default levels, and an optional Chrome-tracing-compatible event printer for visualising worker activity. The discipline is to crash forcefully on bug-shaped failures and recover gracefully on world-shaped failures, with the line between the two made visible by the choice of mechanism.

17.9 Reading exercises






ImportantReading exercise 17.1: cause an exception



Submit a query with an unknown source type:
CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE FOR demo TYPE InvalidType SET();
You should see an UnknownSourceType exception (code 2017). Where in the binder is the type validated? Trace through the function from the binding error to the user-visible message.

Find a place in the codebase that calls INVARIANT with a condition you can intentionally violate (e.g., a debug-only sanity check). In a debug build, modify the surrounding code to violate it. Run a query. The engine should crash with a stack trace. The exit is intentional and informative — that is the whole point of INVARIANT.

18.1 18.1 The worker process
So far, every chapter has been about what runs inside the engine. This chapter is about how a user gets queries into the engine — through what processes, over what protocols, in what shape.
Three pieces:
All three communicate over gRPC. We will walk through each.
The worker binary is nes-single-node-worker. Its main entry point lives in nes-single-node-worker/src/SingleNodeWorker.cpp. On startup it:
The single class SingleNodeWorker orchestrates the engine’s core. Its main public surface is the registerQuery method:
The function takes a LogicalPlan (already parsed and bound by the client) and returns either a QueryId (success) or an Exception (failed compilation). The compiled plan is stored in the engine’s catalog; subsequent startQuery and stopQuery calls reference it by QueryId.
The worker is a single-process, multi-threaded design. There is no daemon-and-workers split inside a single worker. One nes-single-node-worker process can run as a stand-alone engine (everything in one process) or as one node in a distributed deployment, where multiple workers are coordinated by a separate Rust coordinator (Chapter 19). The gRPC API on port 8080 is the same in both modes; the only difference is whether the worker is reachable to other workers via the nes-network channels.

text:
18.3 18.3 Where binding happens
A query in NebulaStream is bound on the client side, not the server side. The client (the REPL or the CLI) parses the SQL, binds against its local copy of the source/sink catalog, and sends the worker a serialised LogicalPlan.
This is unusual. Most database systems bind on the server, where the catalog lives authoritatively. NebulaStream’s choice flips the arrangement: the catalog is conceptually authoritative on the worker (it owns the engine’s running state), but binding can run on either side because catalog updates flow both ways via gRPC.
The benefit is that the gRPC API can ingest fully-typed plans with no further validation needed. The cost is that the client needs a recent view of the catalog. In the single-node deployment we have today, the cost is essentially zero (catalog is local to the same machine). In a future distributed deployment, the cost becomes non-trivial — the catalog has to be replicated to wherever the binding happens.

18.6 18.6 The configuration system
A short note on the infrastructure that all of the above is configured through. The nes-configurations/ module supplies a small visitor-based configuration framework — BaseConfiguration and a family of typed options (ScalarOption, EnumOption, SequenceOption) plus validators (IpValidation, BooleanValidation, etc.). Both command-line flags and YAML configuration files map onto the same option tree, so a worker configuration that lives in a YAML file can be overridden on the command line with no syntactic difference.
This is what --worker.default_query_execution.execution_mode=INTERPRETER in our exercises throughout the book actually does: walks the SingleNodeWorkerConfiguration tree and sets one EnumOption<ExecutionMode> leaf. The same mechanism powers the coordinator’s configuration in distributed deployments (Chapter 19).
The dependence on a generic configuration framework rather than ad-hoc parsing makes it cheap to add new options as the engine grows; almost every chapter that has introduced a “configurable” concept (buffer pool size, watermark slack, network thread count) is plumbed through this same machinery.

18.8 Summary
NebulaStream’s worker is a single C++ process (nes-single-node-worker) exposing five gRPC methods: register, start, stop, query status, worker status. title: 19  Distributed Deployment: Cloud, Fog, Edge
text:
19.1 19.1 The five new types
NebulaStream’s vision in Chapter 1 promised cloud-edge-sensor deployments. Earlier readers of this book might have been forgiven for assuming, from the chapter status callouts, that such deployments were research roadmap. They are not. As of origin/main the engine has a working distributed layer: operators are placed across workers by a mixed-integer linear program, network channels carry tuples between them over a Rust-implemented data plane, and the coordinator aggregates distributed query status with a clean precedence rule for failure modes.
This chapter walks through the implementation. It is one of the two longest chapters in the book — alongside Chapter 15 — because distribution is structurally the largest single piece of the engine’s recent evolution.
Five types in nes-distributed/include/ carry the distributed abstractions. The signatures matter because every other distributed component plugs into them.
DistributedLogicalPlan is the post-placement plan. It maps each worker to the local logical plans that will run on that worker, and keeps the original global plan for reference:
A worker’s view of the world is the slice it gets through the operator[] lookup — typically a single local LogicalPlan per worker, but a worker can host several logical plans of the same distributed query if the placer fragmented the global plan that way.
DistributedQuery is the runtime counterpart: it tracks which local query IDs are running on which workers.
The flattening helper iterate() is what the coordinator’s polling loop uses: one pass through every (worker, local-query) pair, collecting status from each.
NetworkTopology is the graph of workers. The implementation in nes-distributed/include/NetworkTopology.hpp is a directed acyclic graph with explicit upstream and downstream edges, plus DFS path-finding:
addNode performs cycle detection and throws InvalidTopology (exception code 2301; see Section 19.7) if adding a node would create a cycle. The DAG constraint matters because the placer’s connectivity check assumes acyclicity.
WorkerCatalog holds the registry of workers and owns the topology:
The version counter is how clients detect catalog changes (workers joining or leaving) without consulting the catalog itself for every operation.
WorkerConfig is per-worker configuration. Its most distinctive feature is dual addressing:
Workers have two addresses. The coordinator uses management for gRPC control-plane traffic — registering a query, polling status, asking for shutdown. Worker-to-worker data flow uses dataAddress. Forgetting which is which is one of the most common bugs the placer guards against; we will see why in Section 19.3.

text:
19.3 19.3 From placed plan to network channels
A logical plan with PlacementTraits is not yet executable. The QueryDecomposer (nes-query-optimizer/include/Placement/QueryDecomposition.hpp) walks the placed plan, groups operators by node, and inserts network channels wherever a parent-child edge crosses a node boundary.
The substitution is local. A logical edge OpA → OpB where OpA.placement == nodeX and OpB.placement == nodeY becomes:
nodeX:  OpA → NetworkSink(channelId, bind=X.dataAddress, dest=Y.dataAddress)
nodeY:  NetworkSource(channelId, bind=Y.dataAddress) → OpB
The two new operators share a fresh ChannelId (a UUID) so the runtime can correlate sender and receiver. Both consult the worker catalog’s WorkerConfig to find the data-plane addresses (not the gRPC management address — the dual-addressing distinction from Section 19.1 matters here).
The result of decomposition is a DistributedLogicalPlan: one local plan per worker, each starting at a source or NetworkSource and ending at a sink or NetworkSink. From here each local plan goes through the ordinary single-node compile pipeline (Chapter 9-12), producing a per-worker CompiledQueryPlan. The coordinator ships each compiled plan to its worker over gRPC.






TipReal-system reference: how Flink does this



Apache Flink’s analogous step is its JobGraph → ExecutionGraph transition. Flink also inserts shuffle/forward edges that map to network exchanges. The differences:

Flink’s placer is heuristic; NebulaStream’s is exact (ILP).
Flink models per-operator parallelism explicitly (an operator may run on N parallel instances). NebulaStream’s placer produces one operator instance per node by default; intra-node parallelism is handled at the runtime level (Chapter 15).

The exact-vs-heuristic trade-off is interesting. Flink scales to thousands of operators per query partly because it does not solve a global optimisation problem at placement time. NebulaStream’s HiGHS solver is fast on small queries, but its 5-second timeout is a hint that the team has not yet stressed it against very large topologies.

19.6 19.6 What landed and what is still in flux
A reader who has gotten this far deserves a short audit of which parts of the distribution story can be trusted today and which are work in progress.
Landed and stable on origin/main:

DistributedLogicalPlan, DistributedQuery, NetworkTopology, WorkerCatalog, WorkerConfig.
HiGHS-based ILP placement.
Decomposition with NetworkSink/NetworkSource insertion.
Rust TCP channel and MemCom in-memory fast path.
Status aggregation with Failed > Unreachable > Stopped > … precedence.
Distributed exception types (PlacementFailure 2300, InvalidTopology 2301, UnknownWorker 2302, DistributedFailure 2303 — see Section 19.7).

Landed but tuning is open:

Cost-model weights for the ILP. The hop-distance objective gets the right shape; calibrating it for hardware-affinity awareness (a GPU operator wants a GPU node) is in progress.
Backpressure thresholds. The defaults are reasonable; per- workload tuning is pending.

Still in flight:

The Rust coordinator integration on the ys-coordinator-integration branch.
Failure recovery (a worker crash today fails the query; Chapter 22 discusses this open problem).
Adaptive re-placement when topology changes mid-query.

Where the earlier chapters of this book make claims about distributed behaviour, those claims are anchored on this chapter’s verified content. Chapter 7’s discussion of watermark propagation is the principal cross-reference: the four-tuple progress identifiers we met there are exactly what the receiving side of a NetworkSource consumes, and the MultiOriginWatermarkProcessor is what synthesises them into a unified progress view across origins from different workers.

title: 19  Distributed Deployment: Cloud, Fog, Edge
text:
19.8 Summary
NebulaStream’s distributed layer rests on five abstractions (DistributedLogicalPlan, DistributedQuery, NetworkTopology, WorkerCatalog, WorkerConfig), an ILP-based placer (HiGHS solver, hop-distance objective, 5-second timeout), a decomposition pass that inserts network channels at placement boundaries, and a Rust-implemented data plane offering both TCP and in-memory MemCom transports. Worker status is aggregated across the cluster with a precedence order that puts Failed above Unreachable above Stopped. The four distributed exception codes (2300-2303) are a thin layer over the engine’s general error model. What remains in flight: cost-model calibration, the coordinator integration, failure recovery, adaptive re-placement.

title: 20  Testing: Unit, Integration, and Systests
text:
20.1 20.1 The unit-test setup
A streaming engine has more interesting failure modes than most software. Watermarks can be off-by-one. Window state can leak. Joins can produce duplicates. JIT-compiled code can produce wrong answers that depend on the input distribution. Without good tests, none of this is caught before users see wrong results.
NebulaStream’s test infrastructure is in three layers:
The systests are the most distinctive piece. This chapter walks through each layer with the most attention on systests.
Each nes-* module that has tests has them in a tests/ subdirectory. The CMake helpers in /Users/zeuchste/git/nebulastream/cmake/NebulaStreamTest.cmake make registration trivial:
There are three test helpers, distinguished by what they link against:
Tests run through CTest:
The discovery is automatic — gtest_discover_tests finds all the TEST and TEST_F macros in the binary and registers them with CTest at build time.
Most operator-internal logic is unit-tested. The pace of unit tests is high; you can run all of them in under a minute.

title: 20  Testing: Unit, Integration, and Systests
text:
20.2 20.2 The systest framework
The interesting layer is the systest framework. Systests are declarative .test files that describe a complete query — schema, data, query, expected output — in a single readable document. The worker runs the query against a fake source carrying the inline data and the test framework checks the actual output against the expected.
A small example:
# nes-systests/tuples/FiveTuples.test
# name: sources/FiveTuples.test
# description: Simple source/buffer tests
# groups: [Tuples]

CREATE LOGICAL SOURCE fiveTuples(field_1 UINT64 NOT NULL);
CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE FOR fiveTuples TYPE File;
ATTACH INLINE
1
2
3
4
5

CREATE SINK sinkFiveTuples(...)  TYPE File;
SELECT field_1 FROM fiveTuples INTO sinkFiveTuples;
----
1
2
3
4
5
Three sections separated by ----:

Metadata (# name:, # description:, # groups:).
Setup + query (the SQL, with ATTACH INLINE to embed input data directly in the file).
Expected output (after ----).

The framework runs the query and asserts the actual output matches the expected, ignoring trailing whitespace.
This format is brilliant for streaming engines. Streaming queries have multiple inputs, time-dependent behaviour, and complex expected outputs that are tedious to express in unit tests. Putting everything in one file — schema, input, query, expected — makes the test self-documenting.

title: 20  Testing: Unit, Integration, and Systests
text:
20.3 20.3 The systest CLI
Systests run through a dedicated systest executable. From CLAUDE.md:
# Build the systest binary
cmake --build cmake-build-debug --target systest

# Run a single systest file
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest -t nes-systests/operator/join/HashJoin.test

# Run a specific case within a file
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest \
    -t nes-systests/function/arithmetical/FunctionAdd.test:1
The :N suffix runs only the Nth query in the file. Files with multiple queries are common — a single .test file might contain five variations on a theme, each numbered.
The systest binary builds the engine in-process and runs each query against the test’s input. Setup and teardown are test-local; failures are reported per-query with a diff against the expected output.
You can pass worker configuration overrides after --:
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest \
    -t nes-systests/operator/join/JoinMultipleStreams.test:1 \
    -- --worker.default_query_execution.execution_mode=INTERPRETER
This is what most of this book’s reading exercises do. Switching between COMPILER and INTERPRETER mode is the primary tool for isolating JIT bugs from operator-logic bugs.

title: 20  Testing: Unit, Integration, and Systests
text:
20.4 20.4 Multi-worker testing
The systest harness supports running queries against multiple worker processes simultaneously. The CI configuration starts parallel workers in Docker containers — vanilla, profiler- instrumented, coverage-instrumented, sanitizer-equipped — on ports 8080, 8081, 8082, 8083. A single .test file’s queries are dispatched across them; the same query runs in each worker and the framework asserts that all workers produce the same expected output.
This is not yet the same thing as a true distributed-systest suite. It is parallel execution of single-node queries against identical-but-instrumented workers, primarily to catch sanitizer-only bugs. Genuine multi-worker scenarios — where operators of one query are placed across multiple workers (Chapter 19) — are exercised through dedicated coordinator integration tests that live outside nes-systests/.
The closest thing to a distributed scenario in the systest suite as of origin/main is nes-systests/benchmark/ClusterMonitoring.test, a multi-stream monitoring workload modelled on the Google cluster-trace dataset. Even this runs single-node by default; the cluster shape comes from the input data, not from running across workers.
Filling the distributed-systest gap is on the engine’s near-term roadmap (Chapter 22 mentions it as one of the items the QueryManager work blocks).

title: 20  Testing: Unit, Integration, and Systests
text:
20.5 20.5 Group tags and CI integration
The metadata header allows tests to belong to groups. The group tag [fast] means the test runs in the fast lane of CI, which executes on every PR. [nightly] (or .test_nightly suffix) means the test runs only on nightly builds. Other tags (e.g., [legacy], [join]) help filter test runs:
# Run all tests in the join group
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest --groups=join
The CI matrix from CLAUDE.md is detailed: every PR triggers format check → smoke tests → full matrix (x86_64/arm64 × libcxx/libstdcxx × Debug/RelWithDebInfo/Release × address/ undefined/thread/none sanitizers) plus clang-tidy diff plus code coverage. The systests run within this matrix; sanitizer-equipped runs catch a lot of bugs that pure unit tests miss.
crumbs: 20  Testing: Unit, Integration, and Systests

title: 20  Testing: Unit, Integration, and Systests
text:
20.6 20.5 Why systests are documentation
The systests double as living documentation of the engine’s behaviour. A new contributor wanting to know “what is the exact syntax for a windowed aggregation” can grep the systests and find a working example. We have, throughout this book, used systest file paths as the targets of “Reading Exercise” sidebars, because:

Every systest file is self-contained.
Every systest file is tested in CI; it cannot be wrong without CI noticing.
Every systest file is a real example of a real query that the engine actually runs.

For an instructor using this book as a course text, the systests are an inexhaustible source of homework: every test file is a small puzzle the student can run, modify, and predict the output for.
crumbs: 20  Testing: Unit, Integration, and Systests

title: 20  Testing: Unit, Integration, and Systests
text:
20.7 20.6 What is hard to test
A few testing problems have no clean solution today:

Timing-dependent behaviour. A windowed aggregation’s exact firing time depends on real-time progress; deterministic tests use synthetic timestamps embedded in the input, but edge-case timing bugs can still escape.
Long-running workloads. Memory leaks that show up only after hours of continuous operation are not caught by tests that run for seconds.
Concurrency bugs in the JIT. Race conditions in JIT-compiled code may not reproduce reliably; ThreadSanitizer helps but is not a silver bullet.
Numerical edge cases in user-defined functions. A UDF that divides by a value that happens to be zero only on one machine’s data is hard to test without running on that data.

The engine compensates with the sanitizer matrix and a substantial nightly test budget, but the testing-frontier problems are real.

20.8 Summary
NebulaStream’s testing has three layers: unit tests via Google Test in per-module tests/ directories; integration tests via nes-coordinator-test-util; and system tests via the declarative .test file format that describes schema, input data, query, and expected output in a single document. Systests double as self-documenting examples and are the primary target of this book’s reading exercises. The CI matrix runs the full test suite across architectures, libcxx flavours, build types, and sanitizers, providing strong coverage even of timing-sensitive bugs that pure unit tests would miss.
