title: 21  Benchmarking and Performance Engineering
text:
21.1 21.1 Conbench: continuous benchmarking
A streaming engine that produces correct answers slowly is, for most workloads, useless. NebulaStream cares about performance deeply enough to track it continuously, expose it through a public dashboard, and run a dedicated instrumentation build alongside the debug and release builds.
This chapter walks through how the engine is benchmarked, what infrastructure exists, and which performance gotchas are worth knowing.
The README points at a Conbench instance at bench.nebula.stream/c-benchmarks/. Conbench (Apache Arrow contributors 2020--) is a benchmarking framework that runs the engine’s benchmark suite on every commit and tracks results over time. The dashboard shows:
This is the engine’s primary tool for catching performance regressions. A bug that drops join throughput by 20% will show on the Conbench graph before it shows in any user complaint.

title: 21  Benchmarking and Performance Engineering
text:
Per-benchmark throughput and latency graphs across commits.
Regression detection (a commit that slows a benchmark by more than a configurable threshold flags up).
Per-architecture breakdowns (x86_64, ARM).

title: 21  Benchmarking and Performance Engineering
text:
21.2 21.2 The benchmark suite
Two locations:

Microbenchmarks. nes-common/benchmarks/ for component- level tight loops. Things like the ExceptionBenchmark.cpp that measures the cost of throwing/catching an exception.
Macrobenchmarks. nes-systests/benchmark/ and nes-systests/benchmark_small/ for full end-to-end query benchmarks. These reuse the systest format from Chapter 20 with one difference: the expected-output section is replaced with a throughput target and the test is judged on time-to-complete rather than correctness alone.

The macrobenchmark suite includes recognisable industry workloads:

Yahoo Streaming Benchmark. Aggregation over a stream of ad-impression events. The classic benchmark for streaming engines.
Linear Road. Spatial-temporal event processing across road segments. From the original Aurora paper.
Manufacturing. Industrial IoT scenario; per-machine and per-product event aggregation.

Each benchmark has a small variant (in benchmark_small/) that runs in CI on every commit, and a full variant that runs nightly.

title: 21  Benchmarking and Performance Engineering
text:
21.3 21.3 The instrumentation build
The repository has four build directories that each correspond to a build type:

cmake-build-debug — debug build with full assertions and TRACE logging.
cmake-build-release — release build with -O3 and ERROR logging.
cmake-build-docker — release build inside the Docker dev image.
cmake-build-instrumentation — a special build with performance instrumentation enabled.

The instrumentation build is the one the team uses for serious performance work. It enables:

Per-buffer latency instrumentation (the four-point latency measurement mentioned in the engine’s recent commit messages).
Detailed per-operator and per-pipeline statistics.
Profiler-friendly symbols (frame pointers, no aggressive inlining).

Instrumentation builds are slower than release but expose the data needed for performance analysis. The CI does not run them on every commit; they are typically used on dedicated hardware for specific benchmarking sessions.

title: 21  Benchmarking and Performance Engineering
text:
21.4 21.4 The sanitizer matrix
Performance work and correctness work intersect in the sanitizer matrix. The CI matrix in CLAUDE.md describes:

x86_64/arm64 × libcxx/libstdcxx × Debug/RelWithDebInfo/Release × address/undefined/thread/none sanitizers + clang-tidy diff + code coverage.

Each axis multiplies the build cost. The full matrix is large and runs nightly; subsets run on every PR.
ASan (address sanitizer) catches buffer overruns, use- after-frees, and memory leaks. NebulaStream’s reference-counted buffer pool means leaks are rare, but ASan still catches edge cases.
TSan (thread sanitizer) catches data races. The two-queue scheduler (Chapter 15) and the lock-free hash maps (Chapter 16) get the most use of TSan. Streaming engines are concurrent by nature; TSan catches what locks miss.
UBSan (undefined behaviour sanitizer) catches signed integer overflow, null-pointer dereferences, alignment violations. Important for any C++ codebase, especially one with hot paths written in raw arithmetic.
These do not run in production builds — sanitizers add substantial overhead — but they catch enough bugs in CI that keeping them in the matrix pays for itself many times over.

title: 21  Benchmarking and Performance Engineering
text:
21.5 21.5 Performance gotchas worth knowing
A handful of subtleties show up repeatedly in NebulaStream performance work.
INTERPRETER mode is 10-100× slower than COMPILER. Mentioned in earlier chapters but worth reiterating: do not benchmark INTERPRETER mode unless you are studying the interpreter specifically.
Buffer-pool sizing matters. A pool that is too small backpressures sources and limits throughput. A pool that is too large wastes memory the engine could be using for hash maps. The default 1024 buffers is a reasonable starting point; the right value for production workloads depends on operator concurrency.
Logging is expensive. TRACE-level logging on a hot path costs thousands of cycles per record. Benchmarking with TRACE is benchmarking the logger, not the engine. Use Release or Benchmark builds, not Debug, for performance numbers.
Sanitizers slow things down a lot. TSan can be 5-10× slower than a clean build. Do not be alarmed if a sanitizer-equipped benchmark shows numbers very different from a release benchmark; they are measuring different things.
The format-conversion bottleneck. For some workloads (CSV- heavy ingestion), the engine’s hot path is in the input formatter, not the operators. Profilers should focus there first.






TipReal-system reference: Flink’s benchmarking



Apache Flink runs its own continuous benchmarking infrastructure (flink.apache.org/benchmarks). Looking at Flink’s numbers next to NebulaStream’s is instructive — Flink, being a JVM engine running in the cloud, is optimised for sustained throughput on a stable cluster; NebulaStream is optimised for low latency in heterogeneous deployments. The benchmarks each system runs reflect those priorities. A horse-race comparison would be misleading; a side-by-side comparison of which workloads each engine is strong on would be illuminating.

title: 21  Benchmarking and Performance Engineering
section: 21.6 21.6 What to measure when starting work
text:
21.6 21.6 What to measure when starting work
For someone about to do performance work on NebulaStream:

Run the relevant benchmark first. Establish a baseline. If you change nes-query-engine/, run the join benchmark before and after.
Use the Chrome trace. Enable GoogleEventTracePrinter (Chapter 17) and visualise. The trace will show you exactly which operators are taking time and which are idle.
Profile with perf or Instruments. A flame graph on the instrumentation build shows where cycles go. Most hot-path surprises live here.
Compare modes. If COMPILER is slow, INTERPRETER will tell you whether the slowness is in operator logic or in the JIT.
Compare commits. Conbench gives you a per-commit baseline. Did your change regress a benchmark? Conbench will tell you.

The engine has invested visibly in these tools. Use them.

title: 21  Benchmarking and Performance Engineering
text:
21.7 Summary
NebulaStream’s performance engineering rests on continuous benchmarking via Conbench, a multi-build matrix that includes debug, release, and instrumentation builds, and a CI sanitizer matrix that runs ASan, TSan, and UBSan across architectures and libcxx flavours. The benchmark suite includes industry-standard workloads (Yahoo Streaming, Linear Road) plus engine-specific microbenchmarks. Common performance gotchas — INTERPRETER mode overhead, logging cost, sanitizer slowdowns, format-conversion bottlenecks — are catalogued for the practitioner. The Chrome trace and per-buffer instrumentation are the engine’s primary visualisation tools.

title: 22  Where to Next: Open Problems
text:
22.1 22.1 What’s left in the distributed story
A book about a research engine has to end with a chapter about what is not yet built. The vision in Chapter 1 is ambitious; the implementation we have walked through is large but incomplete. The honest place to close is where the team is going next.
This chapter inventories the open problems. They are drawn from the in-tree design documents, the CLAUDE.md notes, and the gaps this book has flagged in earlier chapters. None of them is “trivial cleanup”; each is the subject of active research.
The first draft of this chapter named “moving from single-node to distributed” as the single biggest open problem. That description was wrong — distribution had landed on origin/main (Chapter 19). The open-problem list got longer, not shorter, as the all-encompassing item resolved into several finer ones.
Cost-model calibration for the ILP planner. The current distributed planner weights network bandwidth and per-worker load, but the weights are still hand-tuned. Real workloads need hardware-affinity-aware weighting (a GPU operator’s cost differs from a CPU operator’s) and the ILP solver needs to scale to topologies of hundreds of workers, not the dozens currently exercised in tests.
Failure recovery and checkpointing. A worker crash today fails the query and requires re-submission. The catalog infrastructure is in place to make recovery possible; the actual checkpoint-and-replay machinery is the next major work item. We treat this as its own sub-problem in Section 22.7.
Adaptive operator re-placement. Topology changes — a vehicle drives through a tunnel, an edge gateway disconnects — currently fail the query. Re-placing operators when the topology shifts without losing in-flight state is the deepest research problem on the engine’s roadmap.
Heterogeneous-hardware-aware placement. The planner treats workers as comparably capable. Once the GPU/TPU backends mature (Section 22.4), the planner needs to know that “this worker has a GPU” and “this operator wants a GPU.” The placement framework is ready; the cost model is not yet calibrated for it.
Coordinator merge. As of May 2026, the Rust coordinator on the ys-coordinator-integration branch has not yet merged to main. Bringing it across — and the policy work it implies (failover, leader election, coordinator HA) — is on the critical path.

title: 22  Where to Next: Open Problems
text:
22.2 22.2 Multi-query optimisation
The optimiser today (Chapter 9) optimises one query at a time. For workloads with hundreds of overlapping queries — say, hundreds of dashboards each computing a slightly different aggregation over the same input — there is significant opportunity to share work across queries.
The classical approach is multi-query optimisation (Roy et al. 2000): identify common subexpressions across queries, share their computation. A streaming variant is harder than the batch case because the queries arrive at different times and may have different windowing requirements, but the savings can be large.
NebulaStream’s optimiser does not do this today. It would be a substantial extension — a new phase that operates on a set of queries rather than a single query, plus runtime changes to share state structures between queries.
crumbs: 22  Where to Next: Open Problems

title: 22  Where to Next: Open Problems
text:
22.3 22.3 In-network processing
The vision statement promises “in-network processing” — pushing operators close to data sources to reduce the volume of data crossing the network. Implemented to its logical end, this means running selections and projections on the source’s edge device, not the cloud worker.
What is needed:

An edge runtime. A NebulaStream runtime light enough for edge gateways or even sensor microcontrollers. This is not the current nes-single-node-worker (too heavyweight); it is a stripped-down sibling that can run a subset of operators in a small footprint.
Cost-aware operator placement. A model of network bandwidth cost so the optimiser can decide which operators to push edge-ward.
Coordination across the cloud-edge boundary. State synchronisation when an operator moves; reasoning about watermark progress when some upstream is on a flaky network.

The DIMA group has published research papers on each of these; the implementation is partial.
crumbs: 22  Where to Next: Open Problems

title: 22  Where to Next: Open Problems
text:
22.4 22.4 Heterogeneous accelerators (GPU, TPU, FPGA)
Chapter 19 mentioned that GPU support exists as a research prototype outside the main tree, with TPU and FPGA support as aspirations. The infrastructure to add these — Nautilus’s MLIR backend (Chapter 12) and the pmr::memory_resource extension (Chapter 4) — is in place; the backends themselves are work in progress.
Two distinct sub-problems:

Compiling operators to non-CPU targets. MLIR has dialects for SPIR-V (GPU), and prototype lowering passes from Nautilus’s IR to those dialects exist. Productionising them requires substantial QA and likely more research.
Runtime orchestration of heterogeneous hardware. The scheduler today does not know that thread A is on a GPU; it treats all worker threads as equivalent. Heterogeneous-aware scheduling needs new abstractions.

This is a long-term research direction; expect incremental progress, not a single big release.
crumbs: 22  Where to Next: Open Problems

title: 22  Where to Next: Open Problems
section: 22.5 22.5 Adaptive runtime: changing plans on the fly
text:
22.5 22.5 Adaptive runtime: changing plans on the fly
The fifth pillar in the README is “Adaptive Resource Management — Reacts to topology or workload changes without interrupting queries.” Today the engine’s plan is fixed at query compile time; adapting to changing conditions requires stopping and restarting the query.
What “adaptive” might mean concretely:

Re-optimisation on workload shift. A join whose hash side was sized for 1 million rows now sees 100 million rows; the optimiser should be able to swap to a different join algorithm mid-flight.
Operator migration. An operator running on worker X becomes too loaded; the engine moves it to worker Y without losing state or data.
Schema evolution. A source’s schema changes (a field is added). Queries adapt without re-submission.

Each is hard. Adaptive runtimes are an active research area; (Hirzel et al. 2014) is a survey of the state of the art. NebulaStream has not yet committed to a specific adaptive mechanism; the design space is open.
crumbs: 22  Where to Next: Open Problems

title: 22  Where to Next: Open Problems
text:
22.6 22.6 Late-data side outputs
A smaller but practically important gap. NebulaStream today silently drops tuples whose event time is older than the most recently fired window (Chapter 7). Flink, by contrast, supports late-data side outputs — a separate output stream where dropped tuples can be inspected and, if appropriate, re-incorporated.
Adding side outputs to NebulaStream is mostly an engineering problem (the watermark and slice machinery is already slice-aware), but it is a useful feature that is currently absent.
crumbs: 22  Where to Next: Open Problems

title: 22  Where to Next: Open Problems
text:
22.7 22.7 Persistent state and checkpointing
Chapter 16’s discussion of stateful operators noted that NebulaStream’s state is in-memory only; on a worker crash, all state is lost. Production streaming engines almost universally support checkpointing — periodic snapshots of state to durable storage that can be replayed after a crash to resume the query at the most recent checkpoint.
Adding checkpointing requires:

A serialisation format for hash maps and PagedVectors.
A coordination protocol that briefly pauses tuple processing long enough to take a consistent snapshot (the Chandy-Lamport algorithm (Chandy and Lamport 1985) in some adapted form).
A storage abstraction for the snapshots — local filesystem, S3, etc.
A recovery path that reads the snapshot and brings up the query at the right point in its history.

This is a substantial undertaking and partly intersects with the distributed-execution work — checkpointing is more useful when distribution is the default.
crumbs: 22  Where to Next: Open Problems

title: 22  Where to Next: Open Problems
text:
22.8 22.8 The list goes on
There is more. Briefly:

Streaming SQL extensions — MATCH_RECOGNIZE for pattern detection, more sophisticated session-window definitions.
More plugin extension points — user-defined functions, user-defined window types, user-defined aggregations.
Better observability — structured query plans visualised in real time; predictive alerts on performance regressions.
Cost-based optimisation — when the rule-based optimiser of Chapter 9 stops being enough.
Approximate-query support — sketches, count-min, HyperLogLog as first-class operators.

Each of these would expand the engine’s capability surface; none is a single-PR change.
crumbs: 22  Where to Next: Open Problems

title: 22  Where to Next: Open Problems
text:
22.9 Summary
NebulaStream is a research engine with a substantial implementation behind it and a substantial implementation ahead. The largest open problem is full distributed execution (a QueryManager, inter-worker communication, fault recovery), with multi-query optimisation, in-network processing, accelerator backends, adaptive runtime, late-data side outputs, and checkpointing following close behind. The vision in Chapter 1 maps cleanly onto this list of work; the gap between vision and implementation is the engine’s research agenda.

title: Building NebulaStream
text:
A.1 The Nix flake
This appendix walks through three supported ways to build NebulaStream from source: the Nix flake, the Docker development container, and a local build with vcpkg. The official source of truth is the README; this appendix summarises the steps in book form for the reader who wants to build the engine while reading.
The toolchain requirements are stringent: Clang 19 is the only supported compiler. This is documented in CLAUDE.md; the Nix and Docker paths take care of installing the right toolchain automatically.
If you have Nix installed with flakes enabled, this is the path of least friction:
The Nix flake (flake.nix at the repo root) pins every dependency: LLVM 19, Folly, ANTLR4, simdjson, fmt, spdlog, and so on. Builds are reproducible across machines.
For formatting and clang-tidy fixes:

title: Building NebulaStream
text:
# One-time IDE setup (also creates the cmake-build-debug directory)
nix run .#clion-setup

# Configure the build
./.nix/nix-cmake.sh \
    -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug \
    -G Ninja \
    -S . -B cmake-build-debug

# Build everything
./.nix/nix-cmake.sh --build cmake-build-debug

# Run tests
./.nix/ctest --test-dir cmake-build-debug -j


nix run .#format
nix run .#clang-tidy

title: Building NebulaStream
text:
A.2 The Docker dev image
If Nix is not available, the Docker development image is the next best option. It uses the same toolchain pinned the same way:
# Build (or pull) the local development image
./scripts/install-local-docker-environment.sh

# Configure
docker run \
    --workdir $(pwd) \
    -v $(pwd):$(pwd) \
    nebulastream/nes-development:local \
    cmake -B cmake-build-debug

# Build
docker run \
    --workdir $(pwd) \
    -v $(pwd):$(pwd) \
    nebulastream/nes-development:local \
    cmake --build cmake-build-debug -j

# Test
docker run \
    --workdir $(pwd) \
    -v $(pwd):$(pwd) \
    nebulastream/nes-development:local \
    ctest --test-dir cmake-build-debug -j
The verbose docker run invocation can be aliased to a single command in your shell config; the README has notes on doing so.

title: Building NebulaStream

A.3 Local build with vcpkg
For a local build with neither Nix nor Docker, vcpkg manages dependencies. The manifest is at vcpkg/vcpkg.json. You will need:

Clang 19.

# Build

Pick Release for production. Pick Benchmark only for performance experiments where you understand exactly what you are measuring.
The cmake-build-instrumentation directory referenced in Chapter 21 is a separate build type for performance instrumentation work; the team’s CMake helpers handle it through the build type mechanism.

title: Building NebulaStream
text:
A.5 Common targets
A few build targets you will use repeatedly:
# Build everything
cmake --build cmake-build-debug -j

# Build a single module
cmake --build cmake-build-debug -j --target nes-query-optimizer

# Build the systest binary
cmake --build cmake-build-debug --target systest

# Build the worker process
cmake --build cmake-build-debug -j --target nes-single-node-worker

# Build the REPL and CLI
cmake --build cmake-build-debug -j --target nes-repl nebuli

# Format the entire codebase
cmake --build cmake-build-debug --target format

# Check format without modifying
cmake --build cmake-build-debug --target check-format
The format and check-format targets are required to pass before any PR can merge.

title: Coding Conventions
text:
B.1 Formatting
A condensed reference of NebulaStream’s C++ conventions, intended to make code listings throughout the book self-explanatory. The authoritative source is /Users/zeuchste/git/nebulastream/docs/coding_guidelines.md (~346 lines) and docs/naming_conventions.md (~60 lines); this appendix summarises.
The format and check-format CMake targets enforce this.

title: Coding Conventions
text:
clang-format-19, WebKit-based style.
140-column line limit. Generous compared to the typical 80 or 100; the team prefers to break long expressions only when unavoidable.
4-space indent. Spaces, not tabs.
#pragma once for header guards; no include guards.
Angle brackets (#include <foo/Bar.hpp>) for all includes; never relative paths (#include "../bar.hpp").
No using namespace in global scope of headers. Avoids cross-translation-unit name pollution.

title: Coding Conventions
text:
B.2 Naming

Classes/structs: CamelCase (e.g., QueryOptimizer, TupleBuffer, WindowedAggregationLogicalOperator).
Methods, functions, variables, parameters: camelBack (e.g., optimize(), logicalPlan, queryId).
Enum classes: the enum and its entries are both CamelCase (e.g., enum class Color : int8_t { Red, Green };).
Constants: UPPER_CASE (e.g., INVALID_QUERY_ID, DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE).
Type specialisations: {Spec}{Interface} pattern. A Source implementation for files is FileSource; a Sink implementation for printing is PrintSink. The pattern makes plugin types greppable.

title: Coding Conventions
text:
B.3 Error handling

Bugs: INVARIANT and PRECONDITION macros (Chapter 17). Compiled out in Release and Benchmark builds via #define NO_ASSERT.
Recoverable errors: throw exceptions (by value), catch by const&. Typed exceptions only.
Expected-but-unsuccessful outcomes: std::expected<T, Exception> or std::optional<T>.
All exception types live in a single file: nes-common/include/ExceptionDefinitions.inc. Do not define exceptions elsewhere.

title: Coding Conventions
text:
B.4 Ownership

Prefer value semantics by default. Pass-by-value, return-by- value, prefer composition over containment-by-pointer.
unique_ptr for exclusive ownership. The default for performance-critical code that needs heap allocation.
shared_ptr only where ownership is genuinely shared. The atomic refcount is not free; use sparingly.
No raw new or malloc. No raw pointers for ownership. Raw pointers are non-owning observers.
static_cast / dynamic_cast, never C-style casts.

title: Coding Conventions
section: B.5 Const-correctness and const by default
text:
B.5 Const-correctness and const by default

const by default — Rust-like. Mark variables const unless they need to mutate. Mark methods const unless they modify state.
Pass const& for non-trivial types that the function does not need to mutate.
Return const& only when you can guarantee the lifetime of the referenced object. Otherwise return by value.

title: Coding Conventions
text:
B.6 Other

Operator overloads (+, -, <<) preferred over named methods (add(), toString()) where natural. The << operator for stream output is the canonical “to-string” mechanism.
NAMEOF_TYPE(T) instead of typeid(T).name(). Avoids RTTI dependencies.
Structs for POD; classes for anything with non-public members. A type with private state is a class; a type that is just data is a struct.

title: Glossary
text:
WarningStatus: stub — populated as chapters are drafted






AdmissionQueue. Bounded MPMC queue used by sources, query starts and query stops to inject tasks into the engine. Backpressure surface. See 15.3 Solving P2: a separate admission queue.
Coordinator. A separate process (Rust-implemented, currently on the ys-coordinator-integration branch) that accepts queries, runs the distributed planner, distributes per-worker subplans, and coordinates lifecycle across workers. Chapter 19.
DistributedLogicalPlan. A LogicalPlan whose operators are tagged with placement — which worker each operator belongs to. Output of the distributed planner. See nes-distributed/.
DistributedQuery. Runtime representation of a query whose operators run on multiple workers. See nes-distributed/.
BIFOLD. Berlin Institute for the Foundations of Learning and Data. Hosts the joint research project under which NebulaStream is developed.
BM. BufferManager. Owns the pool of TupleBuffers.
Continuation. A worker-thread strategy for handling a full task queue without blocking, proposed in NebulaStream’s design document but superseded by the unbounded internal queue in the current implementation. See 15.2 Solving P1: do not block the worker on emit.
DIMA. Database Systems and Information Management group at TU Berlin.
Frontier. In timely/differential dataflow, the lower bound of timestamps that an operator may still receive. NebulaStream does not use frontiers; see Chapter 15 for context.
ILP planner. The integer-linear-programming-based component that places operators across workers in a distributed deployment. Lives in the distributed planner; consumes NetworkTopology and WorkerCatalog; produces a DistributedLogicalPlan. Chapter 19.
LHS / RHS. Left- and right-hand side, used throughout the codebase to label join inputs.
MLIR. Multi-Level Intermediate Representation. The IR family NebulaStream’s Nautilus JIT lowers to. Chapter 12.
NetworkTopology. The graph of workers and the connectivity between them. Consumed by the distributed planner. See nes-distributed/include/NetworkTopology.hpp.
nes-distributed. Module on origin/main holding the distributed-plan abstractions, worker catalog, and network topology graph. Chapter 19.
nes-network. Module on origin/main holding the inter-worker data plane — Rust channels (channel.rs, memcom.rs) with C++ FFI bindings. Chapter 19.
Nautilus. NebulaStream’s tracing-based JIT framework. Chapter 12.
OP. Operator (logical or physical).
OriginId / SequenceNumber / ChunkNumber / Watermark. The four progress identifiers used to reason about event-time progress and window triggering. Chapter 7.
PendingPipelineStop. A polling task that checks whether a pipeline still has references and re-emits itself if so. See 15.7 Pending pipeline stops: when even two queues are not enough.
SS. StringStream. Used internally for log formatting.
Systest. A SQL-based end-to-end test in nes-systests/, authored as a .test file. Chapter 20.
TaskQueue. The pair of internal-and-admission queues plus the counting semaphore that synchronises them. Chapter 15.
TB. TupleBuffer. The unit of data movement in NebulaStream. Chapter 3.
TupleBuffer. A reference-counted, fixed-size memory region holding a batch of tuples. The unit of inter-operator data flow.
WorkerCatalog. The registry of available workers in a distributed deployment, with their resources, capabilities, and network reachability. Owned by the coordinator. See nes-distributed/include/WorkerCatalog.hpp.
